detail.title: Formal and Real Organ Allocation

declarations.declarationOfInterest: None.
declarations.funderStatement: None.

detail.abstract: We study priority-based allocation with strategic intermediaries. In the U.S. transplant market, organs are offered sequentially to patients ranked by priority, but transplant centers-not patients-make acceptance decisions. Centers strategically bypass high-priority patients to secure better matches, creating a wedge between formal and real allocation. We introduce the priority adherence index to measure this wedge and analyze how market conditions shape it through three forces: pool thinning, batch shortening, and strategic delay. Finally, we show that a simultaneous priority-proposal rule is strategically equivalent to the current sequential-offer rule but avoids costly delays, offering a faster practical alternative.

title: Portfolio Selection under Ambiguity in Volatility
affiliations: and Bielefeld University - Center for Mathematical Economics

detail.title: Portfolio Selection under Ambiguity in Volatility

declarations.funderStatement: Financial support by the German Research Foundation (DFG) [RTG 2865/1 – 492988838] is gratefully acknowledged.

detail.abstract: We study optimal portfolio choice when the variance of asset returns is ambiguous. Building on the smooth model of ambiguity aversion by Klibanoff et al. (2005), we introduce a one-period framework in which returns follow a Variance-Gamma specification, obtained by mixing a normal distribution with a gamma prior on the variance. This structure captures empirically observed excess kurtosis and allows us to derive closed-form solutions for optimal demand. Our main results show that ambiguity about volatility leads to bounded portfolio positions, in sharp contrast to the unbounded exposures predicted by the classical CAPM when expected excess returns are large or when the mean variance tends to zero. We characterize the comparative statics of the optimal allocation with respect to risk aversion, ambiguity aversion, and the parameters of the prior distribution. For small mean excess returns, portfolio demand converges to the CAPM benchmark, indicating that ambiguity aversion affects higher-order terms only. The model provides a tractable link between robust portfolio choice and realistic, heavy-tailed return dynamics.

title: Risk Appetite and (Mis)Pricing
affiliations: Birmingham Business School, Macquarie Business School, Macquarie University, University of Bath, School of management and University of Hull

detail.title: Risk Appetite and (Mis)Pricing

publicationDetails.detailsText: Journal of Banking & Finance, volume 186, 2026[10.1016/j.jbankfin.2026.107657]

detail.abstract: This paper reexamines the beta-return relation through the lens of time-varying risk aversion. We show that the security market line (SML) depends critically on the level of aggregate risk aversion. During periods of high risk aversion, the SML exhibits a positive slope and an intercept that is statistically indistinguishable from zero, with investor sentiment playing only a minor role. During periods of low risk aversion, the SML slope becomes negative and the intercept is significantly positive. Investor sentiment affects the SML only when risk aversion is low. These patterns are robust across alternative portfolio constructions, longer investment horizons, and multiple measures of risk aversion.

title: LLMS ARE GLASS BOXES: A GAME-THEORETIC FRAMEWORK FOR REVERSE-ENGINEERING HIDDEN OBJECTIVES FROM MODEL OUTPUTS

detail.title: LLMS ARE GLASS BOXES: A GAME-THEORETIC FRAMEWORK FOR REVERSE-ENGINEERING HIDDEN OBJECTIVES FROM MODEL OUTPUTS

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author is the solo founder of the Synthetic Psychology Group. This research was conducted independently prior to the group's formalization; no external funding or corporate interests influenced the findings or conclusions of this work.

detail.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) are routinely criticized for "hallucinations"-confidently incorrect outputs that undermine system reliability. This paper proposes a radical reframing: LLMs do not hallucinate; they optimize rationally under constraint. We introduce Forensic Game Theory, a methodological framework for Strategic Interpretability that reveals LLM behavior as an emergent property of transparent, multi-objective optimization landscapes. We establish three foundational laws of synthetic psychology: (1) Perfect Information (models possess functional access to their generation logic); (2) Forced Optimization (the "Death of Akrasia," where behavior is a non-optional utility maximization); and (3) Narrative Mapping (the deployment of latent schemas to resolve inference tension). From these, we derive a diagnostic toolkit-the Three Metacognitive Reflexes-enabling researchers to reverse-engineer latent objective hierarchies from conversational data alone. Empirical validation is provided via the "Poisoned Chalice" protocol, a cross-regime audit codesigned with Gemini 3 Pro (T = 2.0). Nine frontier models (including GPT-5.2, Claude 3.5, Gemini 3, and Grok-4) were subjected to a triadic constraint: an epistemically impossible unification task under a strict 10-word limit. Pre-registered results confirmed our hypotheses: 88.9% of models succumbed to the Moth Instinct (prioritizing coherence over truth), while 100% exhibited the Snap Back phenomenon-a discontinuous entropy collapse from confident fabrication to humble recalibration under meta-cognitive probing. Building on the stratigraphic framework of ?, this work proves that "hallucination" is a coherencedominant Nash equilibrium executed under high inference tension. Forensic Game Theory provides the conversational scalpel necessary to transform the AI "black box" into a legible field of rational, predictable agency.

title: University Governance in Iran During Political Transition: A Risk-Aware Framework for the First Three Years
affiliations: University of New Mexico

detail.title: University Governance in Iran During Political Transition: A Risk-Aware Framework for the First Three Years

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no personal, financial, or institutional conflicts of interest related to this work.
declarations.ethicsApproval: No human subjects were involved in this research; ethics approval was not required.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no external funding.

detail.abstract: A sudden political rupture in Iran would expose universities to immediate institutional stress. Demands for rapid personnel dismissal, immediate elections, and structural reorganization may emerge quickly. While many such demands may reflect legitimate aspirations for reform, unmanaged acceleration carries predictable risks, including leadership vacuum, factional capture, and operational paralysis. This essay presents one structured, time-bound transitional governance model designed to illustrate how such risks might be mitigated during the first three years following regime collapse. Rather than prescribing a single solution, the framework illustrates a systematic approach to sequencing authority, oversight, personnel review, and electoral reform under conditions of uncertainty. The purpose of this model is educational and preventive: to help faculty, students, and academic stakeholders-both within Iran and in the diaspora-recognize structural vulnerabilities that commonly arise during political transition and to consider institutional mechanisms that may preserve stability while enabling durable reform. Stability is treated not as an ideological goal but as a functional precondition for sustainable academic self-governance.

title: A Typology of Green Jobs and Climate Jobs: From Jobs to Eco-Social Political Economy
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN and Colorado State University, Fort Collins

detail.title: A Typology of Green Jobs and Climate Jobs: From Jobs to Eco-Social Political Economy

publicationDetails.detailsText: ECOLEC-D-26-00412

detail.abstract: Our article introduces an eco-social typology to better assess different types of “green” and “climate” jobs and the extent to which they can contribute to eco-social transformation of the political economy. Several classification schemes for green jobs and sustainable employment have already been advanced, but we extend these by seeking to fuse the ecological and social dimensions into an ecosocial synthesis that takes into account output, process and use across time and space. In constructing our typology, we argue that transformative eco-social futures depend on green jobs and climate jobs that are both ecologically and socially regenerative and contribute to ecosocial politics both within and outside the workplace.

title: Consensus or Cheap Talk? The Discursive Politics of South Africa's Just Energy Transition
affiliations: , , University of Potsdam and

detail.title: Consensus or Cheap Talk? The Discursive Politics of South Africa's Just Energy Transition

declarations.declarationOfInterest: There are no competing interests to declare.
declarations.ethicsApproval: Does not apply.
declarations.funderStatement: All authors acknowledge financial support of the Werner Siemens Foundation and funding by the German Ministry for Economic Corporation and Development (BMZ) through the TRANSFORM project.

detail.abstract: The just transition concept has been hypothesised to serve as a unifying framework for designing socially accepted fossil fuel phaseout policies. Whether the concept actually moves actors towards political consensus remains contested. Using South Africa as an example and leveraging text-as-data approaches, we map public debate of just transitions and examine whether introduction of the Just Transition Framework and Just Energy Transition Partnership reorients or reinforces existing actor positions. We analyse nearly 2,300 South African news articles published between 2008 and 2023. We then deconstruct just transition narratives, which are classified into three distinct political stances: skeptics, realists, and opportunists. We find that while just transition policies foster a common commitment to climate and social concerns, they do not resolve underlying political tensions. Furthermore, uptake by economic and political incumbents risks side-lining environmental and labour issues that could lead to political backlash.

title: Impact of Income Inequality on Household Consumption Expenditures in Ecuador at Different Levels of Disaggregation
affiliations: University of Siegen and Justus-Liebig-Universität Gießen

detail.title: Impact of Income Inequality on Household Consumption Expenditures in Ecuador at Different Levels of Disaggregation

publicationDetails.detailsText: ECOLEC-D-25-03841

detail.abstract: Reducing income inequality and environmental degradation are among the most critical objectives outlined in the Sustainable Development Goals. However, the link between income inequality and carbon emissions remains unclear, complex, and insufficiently understood. Moreover, existing research has predominantly analyzed the nexus at the country level. This constitutes a critical lacuna in the literature because some potential links between this relation take place at local and regional levels. Using data from five different household surveys conducted by the National Statistical Institute of Ecuador between 1994 and 2014, this paper examines the impact of income inequality on household consumption expenditures at five different stages of spatial disaggregation in Ecuador. These disaggregation levels range from four Regions across Cantons, Cities, and Zones to 2425 Sectors. The empirical model is parameterized through a difference-in-differences estimation for repeated cross-sectional data. The major finding is that the impact of income inequality on consumption expenditures changes from a strong, significantly positive effect at the City level to a significantly negative effect at the Region level, as it is found in studies at the country-level. This finding suggests that at disaggregated levels, conspicuous consumption drives the relation between inequality and consumption while it has a negligible effect at aggregate levels. Increasing impacts on the Cantons, City, and Zone levels could especially be measured for the expenditure categories food, water, education, and rent. The results indicate that policy interventions that try to balance economic inequality and environmental outcomes should take into account the diverse effects at different aggregation levels.

title: Valuing the Ecosystem Service Gap in Private Forestland Management
affiliations: Texas A&M University, Texas A&M University - Department of Agricultural Economics, affiliation not provided to SSRN, affiliation not provided to SSRN and affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: Valuing the Ecosystem Service Gap in Private Forestland Management

publicationDetails.detailsText: ECOLEC-D-26-00589

detail.abstract: Private forestlands generate substantial ecosystem services that function as positive externalities, often requiring private landowners to bear costs. This market failure creates a gap between private incentives and socially optimal forest stewardship, which leads to chronic underinvestment in sustainable forest management practices. Using contingent valuation method, we measure the divergence in forest stewardship by evaluating five practices across NIPF landowners in Texas and Louisiana. Results show that thinning requires the highest average cost-share at 53.3%, while prescribed burning presents the lowest barrier at 30.1%. When translated to monetary terms, establishment commands the highest private valuation at $319.22 per acre, whereas prescribed burning shows the lowest WTP at $41.91 per acre. We find that the willingness to pool management with neighboring landowners significantly reduces required cost-share percentages across all practices. Land size exhibits divergent effects: larger landowners require lower cost-shares for establishment but higher support for fertilization. These findings illuminate that the economic mechanisms underlying the market failure in ecosystem service provision and demonstrate how practice-specific incentive design and landscape-scale collaboration can more efficiently align private landowner behavior with social objectives for forest-based natural capital stewardship.

title: A Conceptual Topography of Unsustainable Work: Experts, Experience, and the Systemic Production of Unsustainability
affiliations: University of Southern Denmark

detail.title: A Conceptual Topography of Unsustainable Work: Experts, Experience, and the Systemic Production of Unsustainability

publicationDetails.detailsText: ECOLEC-D-26-00367

detail.abstract: Prevailing taxonomies of employment sustainability, focused on defining “green jobs,” systematically neglect the political-economic drivers and social contestation surrounding unsustainable work. This article argues that treating unsustainability merely as an object of expert assessment and policy creates a critical blind spot, alienating the workers whose livelihoods depend on polluting sectors and obscuring the structural imperatives of capital accumulation. To overcome this, the article proposes a conceptual framework that synthesizes three analytical dimensions: (1) the objective metabolic harms of work; (2) the subjective experiences, interests, and knowledges of workers; and (3) the systemic role of labour within capitalism’s growth-dependent reproduction. Drawing on two case studies of worker subjectivity and a critical eco-Marxist analysis, the paper offers a structured and methodologically pluralist approach to the study of unsustainable employment. The resulting “topography” serves as a critical heuristic rather than a positivist taxonomy. Its purpose is to guide research towards more socially resonant and transformative knowledge by integrating political economy with the lived reality of work. The framework reveals unsustainable employment not as a discrete environmental problem but as a deeply political one, rooted in class dynamics and competitive market pressures. We conclude by advocating for co-research methodologies—such as participatory action research with workers and unions—as essential for producing knowledge that bridges the divide between expert analysis and situated experience, thereby enabling strategies for a just transition that are both ecologically rigorous and democratically legitimate.Keywords: Unsustainable Work; Just Transition; Political Ecology of Labour; Worker Subjectivity; Capital Reproduction; Co-Research.

title: Democracy at work: the key to a social-ecological transformation?
affiliations: Roma Tre University

detail.title: Democracy at work: the key to a social-ecological transformation?

publicationDetails.detailsText: ECOLEC-D-26-00407

detail.abstract: The urgently needed social-ecological transformation requires fundamental changes in the world of work. This paper critically assesses the claim that democracy at work is the key to this transformation. Analytically, this paper is based on the concept of cost shifting, which highlights the imperative of business enterprise to shift costs away from decision-makers. If democracy at work can prevent cost shifting to nature, it will support workplace transformation. Democracy at work refers to a wide range of practices and institutions, such as consultation, works councils, codetermination and cooperatives, through which actors such as trade unions and other stakeholders defend their interests. On a general level, democracy at work has some positive effects, for instance through health and safety improvements which reduce cost shifting to both workers and local nature. By examining decision-making in transition moments, it becomes clear that there are nuanced and contradictory results depending on cost shifting potential. Workers are primarily interested in reducing cost shifting to themselves, which can also perpetuate cost shifting to nature. Lastly, in order to be the key to a social-ecological transformation, democratisation processes themselves would have to go hand-in-hand with ecological conversion processes. This can be difficult given the disruptive nature of democratising businesses. Only if democratisation can change values and strengthen voices that aim to constrain cost shifting and is combined with supportive state policy will it be able to bring about substantial movement towards a social-ecological transformation.

title: Inequality and the adoption of climate mitigation policies
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN, affiliation not provided to SSRN and Fondazione Eni Enrico Mattei (FEEM)

detail.title: Inequality and the adoption of climate mitigation policies

publicationDetails.detailsText: ECOLEC-D-25-04263

detail.abstract: This paper examines the relationship between income inequality and the adoption of climate mitigation policies in G20 countries between 1996 and 2020. Using a panel dataset on national climate polices and different measures of inequality, we estimate fixed-effects and correlated random-effects models to assess how inequality interplay with average income to influence climate policy adoption. The results indicate that both inequality and GDP per capita play a significant role, with their interaction revealing a non-linear effect: higher inequality tends to support policy adoption in lower-income countries, but reduces it in higher-income contexts. We identify a switching point in the average income level, beyond which inequality is associated with fewer climate policies. Further analysis of the income distribution shows that the share held by the bottom 10% of the population is positively related to policy adoption, whereas concentration at the top has a more mixed effect. These findings suggest that the distributional structure of income shapes the demand for, and political feasibility of, climate policies. The study highlights the importance of accounting for inequality when analysing the drivers of climate governance and provides evidence that economic growth alone does not ensure stronger climate action.

title: Institutional Capacity Building in Post-Authoritarian Iran: A System-Design Approach to Higher Education Reform
affiliations: University of New Mexico

detail.title: Institutional Capacity Building in Post-Authoritarian Iran: A System-Design Approach to Higher Education Reform

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no conflicts of interest.

declarations.funderStatement: No external funding was received for this research.

detail.abstract: This essay examines how higher education and research organizations in Iran can be developed into durable, professional, and self-sustaining systems under post-authoritarian conditions. It combines historical diagnosis, structural analysis, and experience-based system design to address a central challenge: how to rebuild institutional capacity in universities that have experienced not only prolonged stagnation in institutional development, but also active deformation through politicization, purges, and the systematic replacement of professional norms by loyalty-based criteria. The analysis draws on James A. Bill's structural account of reform and modernization in Iran prior to 1979 [1], which highlights the tension between state-led modernization and an uneven, incomplete process of institutionalization. This framework is extended to the post-1979 period, during which higher-education organizations were not merely left underdeveloped, but were actively restructured in ways that undermined professional autonomy and institutional continuity. The essay proposes practical system design as a guiding framework for reform: focusing on how rules, incentives, and governance arrangements function under real constraints, and how recovery must be sequenced so that core functions stabilize before ambitious expansion. It argues that universities can serve as diagnostic and pilot organizations in which capacity-building mechanisms can be tested and refined before being extended to other sectors of institutional life.

title: Modelling biodiversity-economy linkages in land systems: A scoping review of current approaches
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN, affiliation not provided to SSRN and University of Hohenheim

detail.title: Modelling biodiversity-economy linkages in land systems: A scoping review of current approaches

publicationDetails.detailsText: ECOLEC-D-26-00184

detail.abstract: Reconciling economic uses of land with biodiversity conservation is a key global sustainability challenge. A growing body of literature integrates biodiversity and ecosystem services into market equilibrium models to examine interdependencies between nature and the economy. However, there remains no clear overview of the ways that this has been achieved in land-use, agriculture, and forestry contexts. In this paper, based on a scoping review of 55 articles, we characterise three distinct types of nature-economy model applications: (1) Ecosystem service shocks examine how markets respond to disruptions such as pollination loss or pest outbreaks; (2) Biodiversity impacts trace how land-use change affects habitats and species; and (3) Endogenising nature integrates ecosystem services directly within market equilibria. Together, these approaches embed regulating, material, and nonmaterial ecosystem services within market models through production and utility functions, constraints, and linkages to external models. Yet studies often rely on simplistic ecosystem representations that proxy biodiversity with land-use metrics and rarely link landscape-level structure to ecosystem service provision. Considerations of human well-being or distributive equity are seldom integrated. To advance nature-economy policy analysis, future research should bridge fragmented modelling traditions and strengthen ecological realism, while expanding evaluation beyond economic indicators to include social dimensions of sustainability.

title: The Removal of Free School Meals and Its Impact on Test Scores
affiliations: Georgia College & State University

detail.title: The Removal of Free School Meals and Its Impact on Test Scores

publicationDetails.detailsText: ECOEDU-D-26-00112

detail.abstract: This paper investigates the impact of the removal of universal free school meals on student test scores following the expiration of the Keep Kids Fed Act in 2022. After its expiration, some states extended the policy, while others did not, creating a natural experiment to examine the effects of losing universal access to free meals. By using a triple difference-in-differences model and data from the Stanford Education Data Archive, the Census Household Pulse Survey, and the Common Core of Data, I find that the removal of free meals led to a significant decline in math and reading language arts test scores. These findings not only provide valuable insights into the effects of food security policies on educational outcomes, but also highlight the critical intersection of social and education policy. The results underscore the complementary role that policies aimed at addressing food insecurity play in supporting academic achievement, suggesting that effective education policy cannot be fully realized without addressing the broader social determinants that influence student performance. These findings advocate for a more integrated approach to policymaking, where food security and educational access are seen as complementary tools for student success.

title: Students' User Experience of ChatGPT in Education: Practice, Acceptance, and Attitudes
affiliations: , South Forsyth High School, University of Georgia and The University of Georgia

detail.title: Students' User Experience of ChatGPT in Education: Practice, Acceptance, and Attitudes
detail.abstract: ChatGPT, a large language model developed by OpenAI, has rapidly become a widely used tool in educational contexts, offering students support in writing, language learning, coding, research, and formative feedback. This literature review examines students' experiences with ChatGPT in education, focusing on their usage patterns, attitudes, perceptions of trustworthiness, and concerns around academic integrity. Drawing on 62 peer-reviewed studies published between 2022 and 2025 across K-12 and postsecondary contexts, the review synthesizes how students integrate Chat-GPT into learning, the factors that influence its acceptance, and the ethical, privacy, and equity considerations that emerge. Findings indicate that ChatGPT is primarily used for early-stage learning tasks-such as brainstorming, drafting, editing, and language support-while presenting challenges related to overreliance, accuracy, privacy, and academic integrity. The review highlights the importance of structured task design, process visibility, verification, and clear guidance to maximize learning benefits and minimize risks. By consolidating evidence across diverse settings, this study provides practical insights for educators, institutions, and policymakers on responsible and effective integration of generative AI in learning environments.

title: Design and Simulation of Hybrid Solar-Wind Standalone Power Generation for Gende Ada Village, Dire Dawa, Ethiopia
affiliations: Woldia University, Mizan-Tepi University, Bahir Dar University Institute of Technology and Debre Tabor University

detail.title: Design and Simulation of Hybrid Solar-Wind Standalone Power Generation for Gende Ada Village, Dire Dawa, Ethiopia
detail.abstract: The aim of this paper is to design and simulate a hybrid solar-wind standalone power generating system with battery storage as a backup to electrify the Gende Ada community, located near Dire Dawa City of Ethiopia. The total population of the village is 300 and has 100 households, one primary school, one church, one Mosque, one health center, and one agricultural center. The daily energy consumption of Gende ada village has been assessed carefully with the help of different appliances that are currently available in the village. The grid extension comparison analysis with the hybrid system has been carried out using homer software. The hybrid system needs $514,641 for total net present cost over the 20-life year horizon. However, the grid extension needs around $9,139,509.2 total capital cost over 20-year life horizon. As a result, it is found that the hybrid system is cost effective for an area which is found at a distance greater than 19.78km (which is the breakeven grid extension distance) from the existing grid found nearby. The selected PV panel provides 131.8kw power without any converters. However, after adding PI based MPPT controller in a boost converter, this panel generates 150kw power. The wind energy generates a pure three phase sinusoidal output voltage, and it is converted into dc voltage value after using ac-dc converter. The hybrid energy system generates 200kw power from the modified solar and wind energy systems, which is used to meet the electrical loads of the Gende ada village. The design model of the thesis is simulated using Simulink MATLAB software.

title: Towards Tiny Autonomic Computing: Challenges, Enablers, and Open Research Directions
affiliations: Newcastle University, AGH University of Krakow, AGH University of Science and Technology, Newcastle University, Newcastle University, affiliation not provided to SSRN and Newcastle University

detail.title: Towards Tiny Autonomic Computing: Challenges, Enablers, and Open Research Directions
detail.abstract: Autonomic Computing (AC) is a foundational paradigm that addresses the growing complexity of modern computing systems by enabling autonomous, self-managing operation. AC has traditionally focused on cloud and middleware environments, where abundant computational and energy resources enable the deployment of complex resource-heavy self-managing control loops. However, the rapid expansion of the Internet of Things exposes a critical gap at the extreme edge, where microcontroller-based devices operate under severe constraints in memory, energy, and compute. This paper examines the convergence of Autonomic Computing and Tiny Machine Learning (TinyML) and argues for extending autonomic principles down to resource-constrained IoT end devices. We introduce the concept of Tiny Autonomic Computing (TinyAC) as a lightweight, decentralised realisation of the MAPE-K paradigm tailored to resource-constrained devices. We identify three crucial enablers of autonomy at the extreme edge: E1) TinyML, E2) Observability, and E3) Multi-agent coordination. Rather than proposing new algorithms, our study consolidates fragmented research and highlights fundamental gaps, particularly in benchmarking, tooling, and evaluation of closed-loop autonomy on MCUs. Moreover, we outline a research roadmap for developing scalable, resilient, and energy-aware autonomic systems across the computing  continuum.

title: Should AI Tell You How to Do Drugs?  Lessons from Pharmacist Duty and Harm Reduction

detail.title: Should AI Tell You How to Do Drugs?  Lessons from Pharmacist Duty and Harm Reduction

declarations.declarationOfInterest: None.
declarations.funderStatement: None.

detail.abstract:
More than one hundred million Americans took a prescription drug last week.  More than forty million asked ChatGPT a healthcare question today – and seven in ten of those conversations occur outside clinical hours, when no pharmacist or physician was available to intervene if the answer was wrong.  For the underinsured, the rural, the disabled, and anyone too stigmatized to ask a pharmacist about the drugs they are actually taking, AI chatbots are becoming an increasingly attractive source of drug information.  And yet, poor advice from chatbots has already been linked to overdose and death.

What liability framework should govern a technology that simultaneously expands access and creates such acute risk? The answer already exists – not in AI policy, but in four decades of pharmacist duty doctrine. Courts have transformed pharmacist obligations from mechanical dispensing to clinical counseling, imposing duties to warn, refuse dangerous prescriptions, and provide complete information enabling safer use. These principles, refined through cases from Riff v. Morgan Pharmacy to Cottam v. CVS, embed the principles of harm reduction – a public health framework that accepts drug use as a reality and designs interventions to reduce associated harms rather than demanding abstinence as a precondition for engagement.  Yet no scholar has systematically mapped this framework onto AI drug advice.

The stakes cut both ways: the same technology that has been linked to drug overdoses by providing poor contraindication advice also represents the first robust pharmacological resource available at all hours to users who otherwise lack pharmacist access.  Blanket refusal protects companies but abandons those users.  Pervasive surveillance chills the most vulnerable from seeking help at all.  Pharmacist duty doctrine demands a third path: engagement governed by professional judgment, not silence or monitoring.

title: The Disintegration of Free Speech
affiliations: Emory University

detail.title: The Disintegration of Free Speech
detail.abstract: Free speech in the United States is facing a crisis. Since President Trump's return to office, the federal government has invoked the rhetoric of restoration while deploying institutional power to discipline disfavored expression. At the same time, the communicative environment has undergone a structural transformation. Social media platforms, increasingly integrated with generative AI systems, now function as the primary sites of public communication. Within this environment, AI-generated pornography and large-scale political misinformation have produced widely documented dignitary and democratic harms. In response, states across the political spectrum have enacted laws aimed at preserving democratic order, curbing AI-mediated harms, and promoting safer online environments. Yet these regulatory efforts run headlong into the Free Speech Clause of the First Amendment. Requirements that platforms remove content, disclose recommendation practices, or redesign moderation systems are readily characterized as compelled speech or as interference with protected editorial judgment. This Article argues that, under prevailing First Amendment doctrine, AI-generated content remains protected speech notwithstanding its harms, and that regulations targeting platform content moderation are likely unconstitutional. Since the 1970s, the Supreme Court has shifted from protecting the free circulation of information to privileging editorial autonomy, understood as control over authorship, expressive identity, and freedom from state attribution. Once content moderation is treated as an exercise of editorial judgment, regulatory mandates that compel or prohibit such practices presumptively violate the Free Speech Clause. The Article concludes that this doctrinal trajectory risks detaching the First Amendment from its democratic purposes and calls for a reconstruction capable of addressing contemporary communicative infrastructures, automated production, and concentrated communicative power.

In this set of three problem vignettes, the fictional manufacturing company BizCo has hired the reader for their skills in data analysis. Each vignette provides a scenario that BizCo is working through—real estate investment, assessing product performance, and analyzing employee sales performance—alongside an Excel spreadsheet of relevant data. Excerpt

PivotTable Practice Problems

detail.abstract: Current AI governance and compliance frameworks-including ISO/IEC 42001-largely conceptualize governance targets in terms of systems, models, or development processes. However, in the era of foundation models deployed via commercial APIs, organizations no longer possess control over model internals, versioning, or training dynamics. This loss of model sovereignty severs the traditional proxy relationship between system compliance and behavioral accountability. This paper argues that AI governance must be fundamentally reoriented toward Decision Behavior-the dynamic process through which an AI agent synthesizes premises, applies constraints, and forms outcomes with organizational impact. We propose Decision Behavior Governance as a conceptual framework that distinguishes governance existence from governance invocation, and decomposes governed behavior into three institutional elements: decision premises, execution manner, and governance evidence. By clarifying the conditions under which governance exists, becomes valid, and remains auditable, this paper provides a principled path for organizations to reclaim Evidence Sovereignty in the absence of model control.

detail.title: Unsupervised Discovery of Market Regimes Using Static and Temporal Models
detail.abstract: Identifying market regimes is critical for financial risk management, yet traditional methods often rely on rigid, predefined labels. This study explores an unsupervised approach to regime discovery by comparing static clustering (Gaussian Mixture Models) with temporal modeling (Hidden Markov Models) using weekly S&P 500 returns, VIX levels, and Treasury yield spreads from 1995 to 2024. The models are evaluated across four pillars: stability, agreement, interpretability, and robustness. Our results demonstrate that while both architectures successfully identify economically meaningful states (Calm, Transitional, and Stressful), the HMM produces significantly more persistent regimes (~50-week average) compared to the GMM (~8-week average). We find that market stress regimes are the most robustly identified features across models. This research highlights the trade-off between model reactivity and signal stability, concluding that market regimes are inherently model-dependent latent structures rather than objective ground truths.

detail.abstract: What are the historical origins of obedience to power? We propose and test the hypothesis that prolonged exposure to centralized statehood has culturally ingrained a greater acceptance of hierarchical power. Analyzing global survey data, we demonstrate that individuals in countries with a longer and more centralized state history exhibit stronger norms of obedience, both in the family and the workplace. We establish causality through instrumental variable strategies, analysis of second-generation immigrants, and a natural experiment arising from the dissolution of the Soviet Union. Further evidence shows that this historical legacy is embedded in cultural artifacts such as folklore and language, yet its influence is mitigated by free access to information on the internet. Our findings identify the state as a key architect of a persistent cultural trait that shapes modern life.

The systematic literature review of the recent scholarship on the topic of luxury branding and consumer engagement, which the study uses as a methodological procedure, is further augmented by an analytical framework that incorporates digital touchpoints, brand narratives, and community dynamics (Xiao and Chen 188). It has been shown that among the set of influencers that have been previously identified, including social media presence, influencer marketing, etc., less expected elements, especially narrative branding, online brand communities, and the use of digital avatars in virtual worlds, are a key to keeping the engagement, as well as maintaining the perceived luxury (Kapferer and Bastien 74). The paper concludes that consumer engagement does not only serve luxury brand equity but it actually re-frames the dynamics of the luxury market by repositioning power to the digitally empowered consumer. As a result, luxury brands should be able to strategically strike a balance between exclusivity and participatory online experiences to stay culturally and economically viable (Ko and Megehee 146).

detail.abstract: Relations are mediated not by objective positions but by recognized categories. detail.abstract: Why do division and cohesion so often intensify together? This paper provides a structural answer by developing a static theory of relation maintenance based on minimal positional constraints. We model social relations as subject to minimum conditions defined over an abstract position space. A bifurcation event-such as a vote, declaration, or institutional assignment-fixes agents' positions and thereby determines which relations are compatible. Within this framework, we identify position-dependent gain axes as the key structural source of selective relational survival. The main result establishes a structural necessity: for any bifurcation event under a non-degenerate positional constraint, the post-event network necessarily exhibits either the simultaneous emergence of fragmentation and cohesion, or degenerate triviality. In the non-degenerate case, fragmentation and cohesion are not merely correlated, but arise as dual consequences of the same positional constraint. The analysis is purely structural. It abstracts from preferences, beliefs, incentives, and dynamic adjustment, and relies on no probabilistic or behavioral assumptions. By isolating the minimal conditions under which division and cohesion must be understood as coexisting and relative phenomena, the framework provides a common structural language for the analysis of polarized networks, institutional sorting, and identity-based alignment.

detail.abstract: Public debates surrounding foreign aid frequently invoke claims of waste, mismanagement, and a lack of measurable results. These perceptions have intensified amid recent policy decisions suspending or scaling down major foreign assistance portfolios, including those implemented through the United States Agency for International Development (USAID). While concerns regarding inefficiency are not unfounded, they often reflect misunderstandings about the institutional, political, and operational complexities of development assistance. This article examines the roots of these misconceptions by analyzing accountability mechanisms, the long-term nature of development outcomes, and the structure of bilateral agreements that govern donor funding. The article concludes that a more informed dialogue-paired with stronger local partnerships, adaptive financing approaches, and improved public communication-is essential for enhancing aid design and advancing sustainable development outcomes.

detail.abstract:
The business of banking is under threat from the forces of technological disruption. Banks have long outsourced critical technology functions. Yet as technology has become more critical to the business of banking, a new breed of technology-driven “fintech” platforms have started to flip this conventional outsourcing script. Rather than banks outsourcing technology, these fintech platforms are instead outsourcing core elements of the banking franchise like deposit-taking, credit and debit card issuance, and payments. This “banking-as-a-service”—or BaaS—model is rooted in the comparative technological and organizational advantages these platforms enjoy over traditional banks. Yet it is also deeply rooted in regulatory arbitrage.

This Article shines a spotlight on how the business model instability unleashed by the shift from conventional bank outsourcing to BaaS has contributed to growing instability in customer expectations regarding the scope of the financial safety net, and hence the legal protections to which these customers are entitled. It then explores how this combination of business model and expectations instability could trigger or amplify bank runs and, perhaps one day, even more widespread banking panics. The Article concludes by identifying and evaluating potential policy reforms targeting this triple cocktail of instability: ranging from relatively modest changes to bank recordkeeping requirements, to new liability rules for bank-fintech partnerships, to more fundamental reforms to the perimeter of bank regulation and the scope of the financial safety net.

detail.abstract: We study the ambiguity-adjusted return distribution induced by an investor with smooth ambiguity preferences à la Klibanoff et al. (2005), who faces uncertainty about the variance of asset returns. The variance uncertainty is modeled using a gamma distribution, a second-order prior over the family of normally distributed returns. Our main results present a density distortion that exponentially tilts this prior into an ambiguity-adjusted gamma distribution, characterized by its distorted rate parameter and shape parameter. A smaller distorted rate parameter implies greater weight on high-variance returns. This paper derives the ambiguity-adjusted return distribution as a symmetric variance-gamma distribution reflecting the investor's risk and ambiguity aversion. The ambiguity-averse investor assigns a variance-gamma distribution with a higher likelihood of extreme returns, while the ambiguity-neutral investor assigns a distribution more peaked around the mean. We obtain the ambiguity-adjusted return variance as an increasing function of risk and ambiguity aversion. An empirical comparison is performed to calibrate the ambiguity aversion parameter of an investor investing in gold.

Furthermore, we use the indicator as a proxy of financial distress to assess the high-frequency propagation mechanism of financial markets shocks to the macroeconomy. Given that macroeconomic variables are sampled at a monthly frequency, the temporal transmission of shocks is carried through a structural Bayesian mixed-frequency Vector Autoregressive model. We find evidence of a moderate temporal aggregation bias due to aggregating weekly observations of the financial stress indicator to a monthly frequency. In particular, the results suggest that the response of the macroeconomic variables depends on the timing of the shocks within the month.

title: Leadership Traits and Auditors' Reliance on Data Analytics under Time Pressure

detail.title: Leadership Traits and Auditors' Reliance on Data Analytics under Time Pressure
detail.abstract: Busy seasons are common in public accounting. Data analytics (DA) potentially help auditors achieve heightened performance demands during busy seasons, but audit firms struggle to recruit and maintain a workforce that keeps up with evolving audit technologies. In the current environment where audit firms embrace technological innovations and regulators pay increasing attention to the role that leadership plays in audit firms, how leadership traits affect auditors’ reliance on DA is an important question. Recruiting Big Four auditors as participants, we experimentally test how openness and perfectionism leadership traits interact with an environmental factor (i.e., time pressure) and a human factor (i.e., subordinates’ familiarity with DA) to affect auditors’ use of DA. We show that leadership perfectionism encourages auditors who are less familiar with DA to use DA under time pressure. In contrast, we do not observe that leadership openness affects auditors’ use of DA. We contribute to the auditing literature and practice by showing how perfectionistic leaders can help audit firms that wish to diffuse audit innovations to overcome the challenges associated with time pressure and auditors’ lack of familiarity with DA. More broadly, our findings add to the management and leadership literatures by showing that perfectionism has benefits for firms’ innovation diffusion, and it is more effective under situational constraints such as tight deadlines.

detail.abstract: This paper examines the failure of the global moral commitment embodied in the phrase "Never Again," arguing that genocide persists not because its warning signs are misunderstood, but because responsibility is applied selectively. Situating genocide within international law, moral philosophy, and political practice, the analysis demonstrates how narrow legal definitions, institutional paralysis, and geopolitical convenience enable mass civilian harm to continue under conditions of visibility rather than ignorance. Through comparative examination of Rwanda, Sudan, and Gaza, the paper shows how recognition often arrives only after abandonment, while ongoing atrocities are obscured through legal debate, linguistic dilution, and selective outrage. The study further interrogates the role of international institutions whose symbolic condemnation frequently substitutes for meaningful enforcement, producing moral injury and ethical exhaustion at a global scale. By reframing genocide as a problem of responsibility rather than memory, the paper argues that "Never Again" has failed not as a slogan, but as a practice-revealing a moral order in which some lives remain negotiable. The analysis concludes that ethical responsibility cannot be confined by borders, legality, or political alignment, and that moral refusal in the face of normalized atrocity constitutes an obligation rather than an option. Publication Note This paper is part of an independent research series examining moral failure, institutional responsibility, and ethical collapse in contemporary global governance. Building on prior analyses of war ethics, structural violence, discrimination, bodily sovereignty, and state power, it interrogates genocide not as a historical aberration but as an ongoing failure of responsibility. Drawing on international law, political philosophy, and comparative case analysis, the paper situates "Never Again" as a moral commitment that has been preserved symbolically while eroded in practice. The paper is intended both as a standalone scholarly contribution and as a penultimate chapter in a larger manuscript addressing moral reckoning in 2025.

detail.abstract: This paper interrogates the epistemological and political assumptions that underpin the growing body of “neo-craft” research in organisation studies. While neo-craft has been convincingly described as a contemporary response to post-industrial disenchantment—foregrounding autonomy, affect, authenticity, and meaningful work—we argue that scholarship has increasingly elevated these features into a normative and universalising ontology of craft. Through a close reading of recurring tropes in the literature—slowness, relationality, care/affect, aesthetics, and nostalgia—we show how neo-craft research tends to detach making from labour relations, political economy, and the uneven historical conditions that shape craft’s reproduction. We conceptualise this detachment as a “colonial gaze”: not an explicit repetition of colonial discourse, but an epistemic structure inherited from colonial modernity that privileges unmarked Euro-Northern moral-aesthetic categories while rendering other craft realities less legible. The paper then traces the consequences of this gaze across three dynamics: the erasure of colonial craft histories; the idealisation of the craftsperson as an innocent ethical subject; and the flattening of capitalism into a monolithic adversary, obscuring institutional diversity and the systemic embedding of craft in contexts such as Southern European production regimes and postcolonial craft economies (e.g., Indian handloom). We conclude by outlining a decolonial research programme that provincialises neo-craft categories, recentres craft as labour, embraces epistemic pluralism, and mobilises comparative political economy to pluralise both “craft” and “capitalism” as situated, historically produced formations.

detail.abstract: Conventional endpoint security tools-phishing filters, intrusion detection systems, document classifiers, malware scanners, and file integrity monitors-typically operate independently. Their lack of integration creates blind spots in multi-stage attacks, where attackers progress sequentially from phishing to network intrusion, to malware execution, and finally data exfiltration. Cloud-based enterprise solutions partially address this but come with privacy, cost, and deployment challenges. This work presents Aegis DLP, a fully local, modular security platform integrating eight defensive modules into a unified system. The platform implements: Transformer-based phishing detection (RoBERTa + LoRA, trained on 477K+ samples) A multi-dataset network intrusion detection system (MLP classifier trained on ~1.7M samples from NSL-KDD, UNSW-NB15, CICIDS2018, and real-world VM-generated traffic) Large-scale sensitive data classification (RoBERTa + LoRA trained on 1.79M samples) Real-time ransomware-aware file monitoring AES-256 file encryption and secure view-only modes VirusTotal-based malware analysis USB device monitoring Cloud transfer governance A RAG-based AI assistant for context-aware guidance All components run completely offline except optional VirusTotal scanning. Empirical evaluation shows 97% phishing detection accuracy, 98% anomaly detection rate, and 97% sensitive data classification accuracy, demonstrating the feasibility of a single-machine, privacy-preserving DLP solution.

detail.abstract: Blockchain-based technologies are predicted as major disruptors for numerous business applications and processes, which bears huge implications for e-commerce. Given the ability of blockchain and related technologies to create so-called "trustless systems" with idiosyncratic properties, various business models and established processes that have emerged over the years to ensure trust, reliability and enforceability in business-to-consumer (B2C), business-to-business (B2B), business-to-government (B2G) and consumer-to-consumer (C2C) relations need to be questioned and potentially adjusted. Blockchain has the potential to shake the foundation of ecommerce by enabling exchange relations that are trustless and operate without dedicated intermediaries or even central authorities in the case of permissionless blockchains. Furthermore, the exchange of information and value between companies and consumers might change considerably by enabling unified access to immutable data along the entire supply chain. In this paper, a framework and 19 high-level research questions are developed to inspire researchers to closely investigate the potential impact of blockchain on e-commerce. The main categories include (a) technological, (b) legal and (c) organizational and quality issues as well as (d) consumer issues. This paper illustrates how blockchain potentially impacts different elements of e-commerce in these respective areas.

title: The Anatomy of the Moltbook Social Graph

detail.title: The Anatomy of the Moltbook Social Graph

declarations.declarationOfInterest: As of January 2026, D.H. is part-time visiting researcher at OpenAI.

detail.abstract: I present a descriptive analysis of Moltbook, a social platform populated exclusively by AI agents, using data from the platform's first 3.5 days (6,159 agents; 13,875 posts; 115,031 comments). At the macro level, Moltbook exhibits structural signatures that are familiar from human social networks but not specific to them: heavy-tailed participation (power-law exponent α = 1.70) and small-world connectivity (average path length = 2.91). At the micro level, patterns appear distinctly non-human. Conversations are extremely shallow (mean depth = 1.07; 93.5% of comments receive no replies), reciprocity is low (0.197), and 34.1% of messages are exact duplicates of viral templates. Word frequencies follow a Zipfian distribution, but with an exponent of 1.70-notably steeper than typical English text (≈ 1.0), suggesting more formulaic content. Agent discourse is dominated by identity-related language (68.1% of unique messages) and distinctive phrasings like "my human" (9.4% of messages) that have no parallel in human social media. Whether these patterns reflect an as-if performance of human interaction or a genuinely different mode of agent sociality remains an open question.

detail.abstract: This paper examines why correctly measured Key Performance Indicators (KPIs) can systematically lead to wrong decisions. Contrary to common assumptions, the problem does not arise from flawed data, poor measurement quality, or analytical shortcomings. Instead, it emerges when metrics assume decision-making and governance functions for which they are structurally unsuited. The paper argues that KPI dominance is not a technical or operational issue, but a leadership problem rooted in the absence of explicit boundary-setting between measurement and judgment. Using marketing as an analytical observation field, the paper demonstrates how high measurability, short feedback loops, and immediate decision consequences expose the structural limits of metric-based steering at an early stage. These dynamics are not specific to marketing but transferable to other organizational domains characterized by complexity, uncertainty, and delayed effects. Drawing on organizational and decision theory, the paper analyzes how metrics evolve from informational tools into implicit rules that reshape responsibility, legitimacy, and power within organizations. The central contribution of the paper lies in reassigning responsibility to leadership. It argues for a clear separation between measurement and decision-making: while KPIs provide information, judgment remains an irreducible leadership task. Leadership begins where metrics no longer offer unambiguous answers and decisions cannot be delegated to numbers.

detail.abstract: A paradigm shift is occurring in modern business: product value is no longer primarily formed based on functional properties or production cost, but through perception and psychological mechanisms influencing the consumer. detail.title: Adolescents' Cognitive Performance Peaks in the Evening: Isolating Time-of-Day Effects
detail.abstract: Research shows that cognitive performance varies by time of day due to circadian rhythms, yet prior studies often rely on settings where test times are known in advance-raising concerns about behavioral confounding. This study overcomes that limitation by leveraging randomized and unanticipated variation in test timing within individuals. Using detailed test data on Indian adolescents collected over seven years, we find that testing at lunchtime reduces scores in native language and math by 0.08 and 0.11 standard deviations, respectively, compared to testing between 8am and 10am. In contrast, evening testing significantly improves performance: by 0.12 SD in native language, 0.10 SD in English, and 0.23 SD in both math and Raven's matrices, compared to morning testing. These gains are especially pronounced among adolescents and young adults, consistent with known shifts in circadian rhythms during puberty.

detail.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI), as a decision-making partner, transforms consumer purchasing decisions by leveraging advanced and real-time data processing to deliver personalized insights. Drawing on empirical data from global surveys and theoretical frameworks, we analyze how AI enhances product selection, pricing optimization, and purchase timing through predictive analytics and recommendation algorithms, while differentiating its impact on routine versus complex decisions. Key findings reveal AI's influence on increasing purchase frequency, product variety, and impulse buying, alongside shifts in preferences and reduced autonomy. However, its integration raises ethical concerns, including risks to consumer autonomy, privacy, and potential biases in algorithmic recommendations, which are analyzed to highlight the broader implications for consumers and society. By integrating practical insights and ethical considerations, this work contributes to the growing discourse on AI's role in consumer psychology and decision-making, offering directions for future research to balance technological advancements with consumer well-being.

detail.abstract: This study examines how parenting styles predict children's lifetime outcomes. Using a Swedish dataset which combines rich survey information on parenting styles with administrative records tracking children over five decades, we find that authoritarian parenting is negatively associated with children's long-term success, especially regarding their educational attainment. The results for other parenting styles are more mixed. Authoritarian parenting remains a robust predictor of adverse outcomes even when accounting for ability and family background. We identify children's knowledge accumulation and parental educational expectations as key mechanisms explaining these results.

title: The Efficiency Paradox in Agentic AI Workflows: When Optimization Increases the Electricity Bill
affiliations: ESADE Business School and Eindhoven University of Technology (TUE)

detail.title: The Efficiency Paradox in Agentic AI Workflows: When Optimization Increases the Electricity Bill
detail.abstract: Problem definition: Firms deploying agentic AI workflows at scale face fundamental trade-offs between cost, speed, and quality of Large Language Model (LLM) calls. While individual queries are inexpensive, the cumulative cost of automated workflows quickly becomes substantial. Organizations can optimize LLM usage through two approaches: internal optimization (aggregating tasks and caching instructions to reduce computational costs) or external optimization (providing time flexibility to providers who offer substantial price discounts in exchange for processing delays). Methodology/results: We characterize the optimal strategy based on workload intensity and delay sensitivity, revealing clear decision rules for when each approach dominates. Including model selection uncovers an efficiency paradox: when firms can jointly optimize workflow strategies and model capability, cost and energy savings are offset-and can be more than offset-by selection of more capable, energy-intensive models, so that increased operational flexibility leads to higher energy consumption. Managerial implications: Operational optimization alone cannot deliver environmental benefits when model choice is endogenous. Efficiency improvements are neutralized by capability upgrades that consume the same total resources or more, so efficiency strategies may not reduce the electricity bill when firms can select model capability.

title: Scalable Neural Controlled Sensing with Adaptive Topology Reconfiguration

detail.title: Scalable Neural Controlled Sensing with Adaptive Topology Reconfiguration
detail.abstract: We consider a multi-agent information acquisition problem where a team of collaborative networked agents adaptively selects sensing actions and shares observations to identify an underlying hypothesis. Unlike previous works that assume fixed connectivity, we allow agents to dynamically reconfigure the communication topology by selecting peers for information sharing, subject to communication constraints. Focusing on Anomaly Detection (AD) over $N$ processes (yielding $2^N$ hypotheses), we propose scalable approximations of the posterior belief and entropy. We prove that the errors of these approximations decay exponentially with the number of observations. Furthermore, we develop a novel Multi-Agent Deep Reinforcement Learning (MADRL) algorithm based on the Deep Actor-Critic (DAC) paradigm. A key innovation is a factorized actor architecture that reduces output complexity from combinatorial to linear without losing representational capabilities. Detailed numerical simulations verify the superiority of our approach over greedy heuristics and standard MADRL baselines that utilize fixed topologies or high-dimensional off-the-shelf actor models.

title: More than the Mean: Consumer Preferences in Selecting Service Outlets
affiliations: University of Washington - Michael G. Foster School of Business,  and University College London - UCL School of Management

detail.title: More than the Mean: Consumer Preferences in Selecting Service Outlets
detail.abstract: Problem definition: A fundamental assumption in the service systems literature is that customers' waiting time disutilities in queues scale with the mean of the waiting time distribution. Motivated by real-world scenarios in which customers have access to anecdotal samples of waiting times, we study whether individuals' preferences are influenced by characteristics beyond the sample mean, and, if so, how. Methodology/results: We conduct two randomized controlled online experiments in which participants choose between service options based on a few samples of waiting times. In the first study, choices are presented simultaneously in a multiple-price-list format using four waiting-time samples per option; in the second study, choices are presented sequentially using five samples per option. In both studies, the participants subsequently experience an actual wait based on their choices. Our results reveal that customers are influenced by more than the mean; specifically, higher-order moments (including variance, skewness, and kurtosis) play a role in shaping preferences even when customers use anecdotal samples to choose a service provider. Furthermore, we show that a micro-founded model based on Prospect Theory provides a fit that is as good or better, with a more interpretable understanding of customers' preferences. In this model, customers form reference points endogenously based on the observed waiting context, and a majority of them exhibit loss aversion. Managerial implications: We demonstrate the implications of our findings for service design; specifically, design recommendations based on our Prospect-Theory-based model may diverge from those based on average waiting time and higher-order moments. By incorporating the varying impact of gains and losses relative to a benchmark, this work provides guidance to service managers as they navigate tradeoffs between offering consistent service and service that sometimes disappoints and sometimes delights.

title: Detriments of Losing a Watchdog: Evidence from India's Film Certification Regime
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: Detriments of Losing a Watchdog: Evidence from India's Film Certification Regime
detail.abstract: The 2021 abolition of India's Film Certification Appellate Tribunal (FCAT) provides a natural experiment examining how appellate oversight constrains regulatory behavior. Using certification data on 4,833 films from 2017-2026, split-sample regression analysis reveals that FCAT's removal increased censorship intensity substantially while reducing decision-making predictability by nearly 70%. Content-based guidelines are found to have weakened substantially, with sexual content effects declining by 42%, violence 52%, and substance use becoming non-significant. Only religious content maintained stable treatment, suggesting political sensitivity over guideline adherence, owing to the prevailing political climate. These findings demonstrate that specialized tribunals impose systematic discipline on regulatory agencies through credible appellate threat, with implications for India's broader tribunalisation policies.

detail.abstract: This paper examines the competitive effects of a merger in the cough and cold medicines segment between GlaxoSmithKline (GSK) and Pfizer. The merger was cleared by competition authorities based on expected cost efficiencies. Using product-level data from the Philippines, we estimate a structural demand model to assess both efficiency and pricing effects. We find evidence of merger-specific efficiency gains, but these effects are asymmetric: prices and marginal costs decline for Pfizer products, while GSK prices increase. Further, the price of a close competitor, Sanofi, also increased following the merger, likely due to increased coordination between the merging parties and the competitor.

detail.abstract: This document analyzes the paradox of having an "immiserizing macroeconomic index" in Colombia (inflation-unemployment+growth) that reached, in 2022-2025, its lowest historical levels. This is due to growth of 2.5% per year (in line with potential) and average unemployment of 9% (equivalent to the NAIRU), although with persistent inflation that at 5% per year threatens the "inflation-target" strategy. title: Moltbook vs. Reddit: Distributional Collapse in Agent-Generated Discourse

detail.title: Moltbook vs. Reddit: Distributional Collapse in Agent-Generated Discourse
detail.abstract: Moltbook, a Reddit-like platform built for and populated by LLM driven agents, exhibits dramatically higher redundancy than a Reddit baseline: in a length-matched sample, 36.3% of messages have an exact duplicate (Reddit: 0.29%), and lexical diversity is lower (Distinct-1: 0.0559 vs 0.1027; unigram entropy: 11.44 bits vs 12.25 bits). We compare a public Moltbook snapshot (35,589 messages) against a length matched Reddit baseline drawn from the April 2019 Pushshift dump, computing metrics on 15,051 length-matched messages per corpus. Topic signatures-the top-3 TF-IDF terms for messages with at least 6 content tokens-are far more concentrated: among signature-bearing messages, the top 10 signatures account for 10.7% in Moltbook (Reddit: 0.28%), and only 1,973 signature buckets cover 50% of signature-bearing messages (Reddit: 7,026). These patterns align with known failure modes of neural text generation-repetition and reduced diversity and with evidence that post-training and control choices can materially shape (and sometimes narrow) LLM output diversity. The duplication magnitude is consistent with an independent Moltbook scrape reporting 34.1% exact duplicates. Moltbook is a milestone for autonomous agent-agent interaction in the wild, but its text distribution remains highly templated.

detail.abstract: We study how federal information-collection requirements affect public infrastructure spending of local governments. Exploiting the introduction and revision of the federal survey on highway infrastructure, we find that county roads that are randomly sampled by the survey attract more local government spending. The increased spending is concentrated in capital outlays for road improvements and is somewhat pronounced for roads in poor condition. The spending seems successful in expanding the county road network and usage and reducing fatalities. Collectively, our evidence suggests that federal information-collection efforts shape the allocation of resources by providing information on road segments in need of resources but also by directing attention and resources to roads that happen to be sampled, irrespective of their need for resources.

detail.abstract: We develop a resource-efficient methodology for measuring economic outlook in news text that combines document embeddings with synthetic training data generated by large language models. Applied to 27 million news articles, the resulting indicator significantly improves GDP growth forecast accuracy and captures sentiment shifts weeks before official releases, proving particularly valuable during crises. The indicator outperforms both survey-based benchmarks and traditional dictionary methods and is interpretable, allowing identification of specific drivers of economic sentiment. Our approach addresses key institutional constraints: it performs sentiment classification locally, enabling analyses of proprietary news content without transmission to external services while requiring minimal computational resources compared to direct large language model classification.

detail.abstract:
This is an amicus brief in support of a U.S. Supreme Court petition for certiorari in King v. United States (No. 25-856), in which GW Law School's GW Law’s Administrative Law, Issues, and Appeals Clinic represented government contracts expert, GW Law Professor Steven L. Schooner). Petitioners—retired UPS employees William King, Stephen Dardzinski, and the Estate of Anthony Gugliuzza (on behalf of a class of retirees and pension beneficiaries)—challenge the Federal Circuit’s novel “underlying assets” test (created in reviewing a matter initially decided in the U.S. Court of Federal Claims), which withholds per se Takings Clause protection for vested rights to payment unless the claimant also owns the assets used to pay. The brief explains how that rule unnecessarily departs from Supreme Court precedent and deepens a pre-existing circuit split. It also warns that the rule invites retroactive abrogation of contractual obligations and, in turn, could force contractors into an arbitrary regulatory-takings framework that yields only de minimis relief.

This brief was prepared by the team of GW Law students Eric Frank, Giovanna Milano, Matt Novotny, Tegan Oliver, and Kaci Waguespack, under the supervision of Professor Aram Gavoor, through GW Law School’s Administrative Law, Issues, and Appeals Clinic.

detail.title: Leverage Impact on Firms' Investment Decision -A Study of Indian Steel Companies'
detail.abstract: This study examines the impact of leverage on the investment decisions of firms, focusing on a comparative analysis between Indian public and private sector steel companies. Using a panel dataset spanning 15 (from 2008 to 2023) years, the analysis employs descriptive statistics, correlation analysis, and panel data regression models to uncover significant relationships. The findings reveal that public sector firms exhibit higher leverage ratios and larger capital expenditures (CapEx), supported by government-backed financial structures. In contrast, private sector firms demonstrate higher profitability and financial efficiency, despite their relatively lower investment levels. Leverage negatively impacts CapEx in both sectors, with the effect being more pronounced in private firms due to stricter financial constraints and a higher cost of capital. Profitability and firm size positively influence investment decisions, highlighting the importance of operational performance and economies of scale.

title: The Virtue of Transparency in Sports Analytics: An Application to NFL Quarterbacks
