publicationDetails.detailsText: MIT Sloan Research Paper No. 7358-26
publicationDetails.journalName: MIT Sloan School of Management Working Paper Series

detail.abstract: A model-based approach to prediction, such as a regression model or a machine learning model, estimates parameters from a sample of observations and applies those parameters uniformly across all prediction tasks. These approaches fail to consider the unique circumstances of individual prediction tasks, and they conceal the influence of observations and predictive variables on individual predictions. Additionally, model-based approaches to prediction offer no guidance about the reliability of individual predictions. We describe a novel model-free prediction system called relevance-based prediction (RBP) that overcomes these limitations, and we show how it enables prediction-specific transparency that is beyond the reach of model-based approaches. RBP reveals the specific reliability of each prediction before the prediction is made, the importance of each prior player to each prediction, the contribution of each predictive variable to each prediction's value, and the contribution of each predictive variable to each prediction's reliability. We illustrate this new prediction system by applying it to predict passing yards per game for NFL quarterbacks. The prediction-specific information given by RBP stands in contrast to R-squared, t-statistics, and beta which only give information about average effects, as we illustrate with specific player examples.

title: Labor Futures Under Artificial Intelligence: Scenarios for the Philippine Economy
affiliations: CirroLytix Research Services

detail.title: Labor Futures Under Artificial Intelligence: Scenarios for the Philippine Economy
detail.abstract:
Rapid advances in generative artificial intelligence (AI) are reshaping the nature of work worldwide, yet their labor market implications remain highly uncertain and context-dependent. This paper examines the likely impacts of AI on labor in the Philippines through a prognostic, scenario-based approach that moves beyond deterministic forecasts. Drawing on three complementary evidence bases—task-level evidence on what generative AI can already do in practice, occupational exposure and complementarity analysis using Philippine labor force data, and firm- and worker-level evidence on AI adoption—the study develops an integrated framework linking AI capabilities, occupational structure, and institutional mediation.

The analysis shows that while a significant share of Philippine employment is exposed to AI—particularly in service-sector and BPO-related occupations—most exposed jobs also exhibit high complementarity, suggesting substantial scope for augmentation rather than immediate displacement. Observed adoption patterns to date are cautious, with limited job loss but growing task reconfiguration and emerging skills gaps. Building on these findings, the paper develops three policy-contingent labor market scenarios for the period 2025–2035: an Augmented Services Economy characterized by inclusive productivity gains, a Dual-Speed Labor Market marked by polarization and uneven adjustment, and a Disruptive Automation Shock involving significant displacement and social strain.

The paper argues that AI’s labor market impacts in the Philippines are not technologically predetermined. Instead, outcomes will depend on policy choices related to skills development, governance, social protection, and innovation. The Philippines faces a narrow but real window to steer AI adoption toward inclusive upgrading rather than disruptive adjustment.

title: A Comment on "Estimating Large-Scale Tree Logit Models"
affiliations: The Chinese University of Hong Kong (CUHK) - CUHK Business School

detail.title: A Comment on "Estimating Large-Scale Tree Logit Models"
detail.abstract: Jagabathula et al. (2024) propose a scalable algorithm for estimating large-scale tree logit models and illustrate their approach using a "SUSHI" data exercise. This exercise generates millions of transactions by repeatedly drawing random offer sets and deterministically assigning each individual the highest-ranked available item (or no-purchase) from survey-based preference orderings. This comment focuses on interpretation rather than computation. I show that the deterministic rankings-to-choices mapping makes conditional choice almost deterministic and, under random assortments, creates a long-tail pattern in which many products are offered frequently but chosen rarely. A binary logit example clarifies the core mechanism: determinism pushes logit estimation into a boundary regime in which the utility differences become extreme and weakly identified, and in the high-dimensional SUSHI construction, this manifests as nearseparation-style imbalance (rarely chosen yet frequently offered items). In contrast, the tree logit model can match the same near-determinism primarily through scaled indices-by pushing dissimilarity parameters toward their lower bound, thereby making implied conditional log-odds large-without requiring comparably extreme dispersion in leaf-level utilities. I therefore argue that the reported likelihood advantages in the SUSHI exercise are best viewed as evidence of performance under a semi-synthetic stress test, rather than as direct validation that the model captures real-world correlations better in transactional choice data.

title: When Perishables Go Online: The Impact on Waste, Welfare, and Profit
affiliations: Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT), Operations Research Center and Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT) - Sloan School of Management

detail.title: When Perishables Go Online: The Impact on Waste, Welfare, and Profit

publicationDetails.detailsText: MIT Sloan Research Paper (forthcoming)
publicationDetails.journalName: MIT Sloan School of Management Working Paper Series

detail.abstract: Reducing food waste, particularly at the downstream stages of the supply chain, has become a global priority. At the same time, online grocery shopping has expanded rapidly. This raises an important question: how does the adoption of online grocery shopping influence food waste at the consumer and retail levels? To address this question, we develop a bi-level optimization framework in which the lower level captures consumers’ repeat-purchase decisions and the upper level models the retailer’s inventory management problem. A key methodological contribution is endogenizing consumers’ purchase behavior in a perishable setting, translating their decisions into the stochastic demand faced by the retailer. To this end, we characterize an asymptotically optimal base-stock policy for the retailer that captures the essential system dynamics while remaining analytically tractable. Our results show that online grocery adoption can reduce waste at both the consumer and retail levels, provided it targets the “right” consumers and products; specifically, it can enable more frequent replenishment by reducing the fixed cost of purchasing relative to in-store trips, with larger gains for products with lower perishability and consumption rates. We also identify substantial overlap between regions where waste declines and consumer welfare and retailer profitability increase, yielding a triple-win outcome. Empirical calibrations using U.S. retail data confirm that lowering the fixed cost of purchase is the primary moderator; notably, a 9-15% reduction in delivery fees can unlock this triple-win across all states in our analysis. This alignment underscores the potential of online grocery to simultaneously enhance environmental sustainability and economic efficiency.

title: The Trilemma, Macroprudential Policy, and Monetary Spillovers

publicationDetails.detailsText: Hong Kong Institute for Monetary and Financial Research (HKIMR) Research Paper No. 20/2025
publicationDetails.journalName: Hong Kong Institute for Monetary & Financial Research (HKIMR) Research Paper Series

detail.abstract:
This research paper is written by Haiqin Liu (Fudan University).

Using hand-dated country policy events and daily firm-level equity returns, I estimate how capital controls, exchange rate regimes, and macroprudential policy moderate spillovers from monetary shocks by the Fed, ECB, and BoE. Exploiting an event-study design around precisely dated domestic policy changes, I show that for conventional monetary policy shocks, tightening capital controls or adopting a more flexible exchange rate regime attenuates negative equity spillovers. This is in support of the classic Trilemma. For quantitative easing (QE) shocks, exchange rate flexibility amplifies positive spillovers. Conversely, capital controls and macroprudential policy tightening can mitigate spillovers from QE. Interestingly, what distinguishes macroprudential tools from capital controls is that, as QE purchase sizes scale up, macroprudential tools remain effective whereas the absorptive capacity of capital controls wanes. These results underscore the central role of balance sheet and risk premium channels in the international transmission of QE. Simulations from a stylized two-country collateral model deliver consistent predictions.

title: Does Mediation Deliver Justice? The Perspective of Unrepresented Parties
affiliations: University of Strathclyde – Law School

detail.title: Does Mediation Deliver Justice? The Perspective of Unrepresented Parties

declarations.ethicsApproval: Ethical approval was granted by Queen Margaret University's Ethics Committee
declarations.funderStatement: The research was partially funded by a doctoral research grant from Queen Margaret University

detail.abstract: This study examines the justice thinking of unrepresented people who have taken part in mediation. The context is two mediation services, serving Scotland’s two largest courts, from which the twenty four participants were referred to mediation by a judge (known as a sheriff) in the course of a small claim. The study addresses a notable gap in the literature on mediation: the modest attention paid to parties’ perspectives on substantive justice (see Chapter 1.C and 3.C. below). Its aim was to provide a richer understanding of the thinking of mediation participants charged by the justice system with devising an outcome to their disputes, in particular their evaluations of the fairness and justice of that outcome. It finds that those without legal training can nonetheless apply justice principles in resolving their disputes; this can be described as “justice outside the law.” They were able to account for their decisions in terms recognisable to those operating the justice system: the encounter (replicating the day in court), the chance to tell their story, compensation, punishment of bad behaviour, closure and payment. However, their lack of formal legal knowledge can lead to injustice and the study highlights the key role of activist mediators in providing legal information when required. Despite having forged the terms of their settlements, most participants were ambivalent when asked “Did you get justice?” The study notes several reasons. First, they are decision makers who are also decision recipients, meaning the other party, their legal opponent, has a say in the outcome. Secondly, they want to do, and be seen to do, justice. Thirdly, they also want to receive justice (and not injustice), yet often have to compromise and settle for “good enough” (see Chapters 5 and 6, below). And finally they have little interest in applying, still less in creating, legal norms. I conclude that mediation can deliver justice but not law.

It further explores the relationship between user satisfaction and future behavioral intentions, including word-of-mouth promotion and continued engagement. All four quality dimensions-ease of use, responsiveness, helpfulness of AI, and reliability-demonstrated a positive and statistically significant impact on customer satisfaction. Furthermore, satisfaction positively influenced users' future behavioral intentions. It provides a framework for public sector entities to assess AI effectiveness in service delivery.

detail.abstract: As artificial intelligence systems transition from analytical tools to operational decision delegates, governance frameworks have not evolved at the same pace as real-world usage. Existing approaches emphasize model correctness, policy compliance, and system integrity, but provide limited visibility into how humans actually interact with AI at runtime. This report presents qualitative validation evidence indicating a systemic governance gap: organizations can increasingly reconstruct what AI systems did, yet cannot reliably demonstrate who owned decisions at the moment of execution or whether meaningful human judgment was exercised. Drawing on cross-industry practitioner perspectives and market-level evidence from Indian enterprises, the analysis identifies human behavioral drift-not technical failure-as the dominant cause of governance breakdown. The findings suggest the need for a distinct operational governance layer focused on preserving, observing, and evidencing human decision ownership in AI-assisted workflows.

This research paper is written by Yuet Ning Chau (Hong Kong University of Science and Technology).

I provide the first causal evidence that settlement cycle mismatch across jurisdictions disrupt arbitrage mechanisms. Using the US transition to T+1 settlement as a quasi-natural experiment, I find that arbitrage activity significantly declines for US ETFs tracking foreign assets. This decline increases tracking error and reduces liquidity for these ETFs. The effects spill over, impacting other ETFs that share the same arbitrageurs and reducing liquidity in the underlying foreign assets. These findings underscore the economic costs of uncoordinated settlement cycles.

title:
The Adaptive Signaling Economy
An Ethological Theory of Human Economic Behavior
affiliations: Independent Researcher

detail.title:
The Adaptive Signaling Economy
An Ethological Theory of Human Economic Behavior
detail.abstract:
LStandard economic theory models individuals as rational agents maximizing utility under constraints. While behavioral economics has introduced psychological deviations from rationality, it still largely abstracts from the evolutionary origins of economic behavior.

This paper proposes a unifying framework, The Adaptive Signaling Economy (ASE), grounded in ethology and evolutionary biology. We argue that a substantial share of human economic behavior is best understood as adaptive signaling, inherited from animal social systems, where economic actions primarily function to signal status, fitness, trustworthiness, and group membership rather than to maximize material payoff alone.

By integrating animal signaling theory, evolutionary stable strategies, and economic choice, we formalize a model in which markets operate as signaling arenas. The framework explains persistent economic anomalies such as conspicuous consumption, unpaid labor, excessive competition, speculative behavior, and reputation-driven markets. The theory generates testable predictions that diverge from both neoclassical and standard behavioral models, offering a biologically grounded foundation for economic analysis.

detail.title: Family Structures and Women's Empowerment in Islamic Societies
detail.abstract: Over the past five years, there has been a growing body of research on women's empowerment in Islamic societies, with increasing emphasis on family structures as evolving social systems rather than fixed cultural institutions. This survey paper reviews interdisciplinary literature published between 2020 and 2025, examining how different family arrangements-extended, nuclear, and single-parent households-shape women's access to education, employment, decision-making power, and social participation. Drawing on scholarship from sociology, gender studies, development economics, and anthropology, the paper analyzes how family dynamics interact with legal frameworks, economic pressures, religious interpretations, and generational change, particularly among Generation Z. The review highlights policy-relevant and practical implications for development practitioners, civil society organizations, and community leaders seeking to promote women's empowerment in culturally grounded and sustainable ways.

title: Work-Related Burnout in Judicial Institutions: Organizational, Institutional, and Human Implications

detail.title: Work-Related Burnout in Judicial Institutions: Organizational, Institutional, and Human Implications
detail.abstract: Work-related burnout has become a critical concern in contemporary judicial institutions, with implications that extend beyond individual well-being to organizational functioning and institutional legitimacy. This article examines burnout as a multidimensional and systemic phenomenon arising from sustained imbalances between job demands and available resources in judicial work. Drawing on established organizational behavior frameworks and empirical research, the study analyzes the organizational, psychosocial, and individual antecedents of burnout among judicial professionals. It further explores the consequences of burnout at multiple levels, including employee health and motivation, the effectiveness and internal climate of judicial organizations, and public trust in justice institutions. The article concludes by discussing integrated prevention and intervention strategies, emphasizing the importance of organizational design, supportive work environments, and ins tuitional commitment to employee well-being. Addressing burnout is framed not as an individual coping issue, but as a strategic investment in the quality, resilience, and long-term performance of judicial instituitions.

title: Deep Learning-Based Fault Detection and Ride-Through Enhancement Techniques in Wind Farm Power Systems

detail.title: Deep Learning-Based Fault Detection and Ride-Through Enhancement Techniques in Wind Farm Power Systems
detail.abstract: The rapid integration of wind energy into modern power systems has introduced significant challenges related to fault detection, transient stability, and grid code compliance. As wind farms increasingly rely on power electronic interfaces, traditional protection and control methods struggle to respond effectively to complex and fast-evolving fault conditions. This study investigates deep learning-based fault detection and ride-through enhancement techniques for wind farm power systems, with a focus on improving low-voltage ride-through (LVRT) performance under diverse grid disturbances. A unified framework is developed that integrates convolutional neural network-based fault classification with intelligent ride-through control strategies. The methodology leverages multi-source operational data and evaluates performance across multiple fault scenarios. Results demonstrate notable improvements in fault detection accuracy, response speed, voltage recovery, and transient stability compared to conventional and shallow learning approaches. Unexpectedly, the deep learning models exhibit strong generalization even under compound fault conditions, highlighting their robustness. The findings suggest that deep learning-driven protection and control can play a pivotal role in enabling reliable, resilient, and grid-compliant wind power integration. The study concludes by outlining future research directions and practical implications for next-generation wind farm protection systems.

title: Intelligent Protection Schemes for Grid-Connected Wind Farms Using CNN-Based Fault Classification

detail.title: Intelligent Protection Schemes for Grid-Connected Wind Farms Using CNN-Based Fault Classification
detail.abstract: The increasing penetration of grid-connected wind farms has significantly altered the dynamic behavior of modern power systems, introducing new challenges for conventional protection schemes (Kandil, Harris, and Das). Traditional relay-based protection methods often struggle under conditions of fluctuating generation, low fault currents, and inverter-dominated responses (Bhalja et al.). This study proposes an intelligent protection scheme for grid-connected wind farms using convolutional neural network (CNN)-based fault classification to enhance detection accuracy and response speed (Dilmi et al.). Voltage and current signals obtained from numerical relays are processed and used to train a deep CNN model capable of identifying multiple fault types under diverse operating conditions (Mokhtari et al.). The results demonstrate that the proposed approach achieves higher classification accuracy and improved robustness during low-voltage ride-through (LVRT) events compared to conventional techniques (Ali et al.). The findings confirm that CNN-based protection frameworks can significantly improve grid resiliency and reliability in renewable-rich power systems (Abu Sarhan).

title: Application of Convolutional Neural Networks for Real-Time Fault Detection in Renewable Energy Power Generation Systems
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: Application of Convolutional Neural Networks for Real-Time Fault Detection in Renewable Energy Power Generation Systems
detail.abstract: The rapid global transition toward renewable energy has intensified the need for reliable, intelligent, and real-time fault detection mechanisms to ensure system stability and operational efficiency. Renewable energy power generation systems, including wind farms, solar photovoltaic installations, and microgrids, are inherently complex and exposed to diverse environmental and operational uncertainties. Traditional fault detection approaches, largely based on rule-based logic and signal processing techniques, often struggle to cope with nonlinearity, noise, and high-dimensional data generated by modern energy systems (Kandil et al.; Negi et al.). This study examines the application of convolutional neural networks (CNNs) for real-time fault detection in renewable energy power generation systems. By synthesizing recent empirical research across multiple renewable domains, this work analyzes CNN architectures, data modalities, and deployment strategies that enable accurate and timely fault diagnosis. The findings indicate that CNN-based approaches consistently outperform conventional and shallow machine learning methods in fault detection accuracy, robustness, and adaptability (Bukhari et al.; Drir et al.; Liu et al.). However, challenges related to data availability, computational constraints, and model interpretability persist. The study concludes that CNNs represent a powerful and scalable solution for real-time fault detection in renewable energy systems, provided that future research addresses explainability and edge-deployment limitations.

Large-scale oil and gas EPC projects executed across Russia, Central Asia, and North Africa are characterized by extreme regulatory volatility, geopolitical risk, sanctions exposure, fragmented governance structures, and chronic execution inefficiencies. Traditional project management frameworks—while formally adopted—often fail to protect capital, control decision-making latency, and prevent systemic waste under these conditions.


This research monograph introduces the Global Risk-Driven Project Delivery (GRDP Model™), an original project governance and execution framework developed through more than twenty years of direct leadership experience in multi-billion-dollar upstream, midstream, downstream, LNG, pipeline, refinery, and gas-chemical projects. The model integrates risk-oriented governance, decision-flow control, lean execution principles, and capital protection mechanisms tailored specifically for high-risk international EPC environments.


Drawing on practical case studies from Russia, Central Asia, and North Africa, the monograph demonstrates how conventional stage-gate, PMBOK-based, and compliance-driven project management approaches frequently amplify execution waste, delay decisions, and expose investors to avoidable capital losses. In contrast, the GRDP Model™ restructures project governance around risk-weighted decision authority, adaptive escalation paths, lean risk buffers, and value-based performance control.


The findings are particularly relevant for U.S. and international companies operating in sanctioned, emerging, or geopolitically complex regions, offering a practical methodology to enhance return on investment, improve capital efficiency, and strengthen execution resilience in large-scale energy and industrial projects.

Bellucci had rejected similar molding-machine proposals for economic reasons on three previous occasions, most recently in 2024. title: A Quantitative Theory of Hierarchical Coordination Ceilings

detail.title: A Quantitative Theory of Hierarchical Coordination Ceilings

detail.abstract: For nearly nine decades, transaction cost economics has explained firm boundaries in qualitative terms: organizations grow until internal coordination costs exceed external market costs. This paper proposes the first quantitative formulation of that constraint. We model the firm as a hierarchical information-processing system subject to semantic degradation, where managers function as regenerative repeaters counteracting noise accumulation. The resulting bridge equation, 1 − κ = (1 − ε)^αd, connects coordination overhead (κ) to hierarchy depth (d), per-level distortion (ε), and organizational coupling (α). Empirical validation across five independent sources—corporate accounting data, developer surveys, knowledge worker time-use studies, and macroeconomic analyses—reveals convergence around κ ≈ 0.40–0.42, consistent with our prediction of a synchronous efficiency limit. A conservation law emerges: viable organizations cluster near εd ≈ 0.50, trading depth for communication fidelity along this constraint. The framework explains why functional hierarchies stall at approximately five levels, why multidivisional structure enables organizational giants, and why remote work triggered widespread coordination crisis. We derive testable predictions about startup scaling traps, merger integration failures, and the coordination implications of artificial intelligence.

How characters, for example, were portrayed in films had implications for how they were portrayed in Disney's parks or translated into consumer goods. Crommett needed to consider the cultural authenticity not only of new creative content (and characters) but also of Disney's past box office hits, which often led to live-action remakes. In the summer of 2017, new to Disney and the studio film industry and attempting to rattle long-held mindsets and navigate new terrain, Crommett needed to plot her next steps carefully.

The Film Industry

The film industry produced, marketed, and distributed films. Films were either feature length or short. Films were financed and produced at one of the major “Hollywood” studios (i.e., Disney, Paramount Pictures Corporation, Sony Pictures Entertainment Inc., Twentieth Century Fox Film Corporation, Universal Pictures, and Warner Bros. Entertainment Inc.) or at independent (indie) studios. Major studio films tended to cost more to make (up to hundreds of millions of dollars), had broader distribution, and had well-known actors and directors. Indie films were made outside of the “studio system,” had much lower budgets, could have distribution challenges, and often featured newcomers in front of and behind the camera. Raising money to produce an indie film could be particularly challenging. Film production could involve collaboration between one or multiple studios, which led to varying project costs and revenues. Distribution of films in 2017 was primarily through theatrical release (i.e., showing films in movie theaters). With the emergence of streaming services (e.g., Netflix), a shift from DVD sales as a key profit maker for the studios was underway.

detail.abstract:
On April 2, 2025 (called “Liberation Day” by US President Donald Trump), the United States announced extensive tariffs on its trading partners. This presented the executives at Caterpillar Inc. with some difficult decisions, as their firm operated around the globe and sourced parts from many countries. Company leaders needed to determine the best location for a new plant while they navigated an unfamiliar international trade environment. Through the perspective of both microeconomic and macroeconomic theory, this case provides the context to analyze tariff policy and firm-level outcomes. The case bridges partial equilibrium (micro-level) international trade concepts with general equilibrium (macro-level) logic. In particular, it enables students to understand the impacts of tariffs on individual markets and countries as well as the effects of tariffs on exchange rates, policy uncertainty, and inflation. Ultimately, students will utilize economic theory to evaluate the current international trade atmosphere and its influence on corporate decisions. At the University of Virginia Darden School of Business, this case is the first piece of a two-class series that covers tariffs and the US dollar. For the companion case, see Felipe Saffie and Bryan Harrison, “Dollars, Debt, and Destiny: Marfrig's Dilemma in a Changing Currency World” (UVA-GEM-0254).

Excerpt

Tariff Trouble: Navigating a Trade War in the Global Supply Chain

In the spring of 2025, the leadership team of Caterpillar Inc. (Caterpillar) faced a crucial decision. The US government had announced extensive new tariffs on products imported from around the world. As the international landscape evolved, CEO Joe Creed and his team wanted to choose the best site for a new production facility. The team needed to consider the potential profitability for each plant location amid the uncertainty surrounding future US tariffs and monetary policies. How would changes in these variables affect the firm's long-term growth prospects? Would a domestic or foreign plant offer the better investment opportunity?

Tariffs and US Policy

Tariffs were taxes levied by a government on imported products. In the United States, Customs and Border Protection (CBP) typically collected the duty on a good at the port of entry. The US importer classified the good based on the Harmonized Tariff Schedule of the United States and stated the value or quantity. Then, CBP examined the applicable paperwork, accepted the tariff payment from the importer, and deposited the money into the US General Fund. In late 18th- and early 19th-century United States, a significant portion of government revenue came from tariffs, but by 2024, less than 2% of taxes collected came from customs duties.

title: How should Macroeconomists think about AI and the Labor Market?
affiliations: University of Trento - Department of Economics and Management

detail.title: How should Macroeconomists think about AI and the Labor Market?

detail.abstract: As generative artificial intelligence (AI) moves rapidly from promise to practice, its early labor-market effects pose a puzzle for economists. Standard frameworks of skill-biased and routine-biased technological change predict that new technologies either complement highly skilled workers or displace routine labor. Yet emerging evidence paints a more complex picture. Recent results from Brynjolfsson et al. (2025a) show that the initial impact of widespread AI adoption is characterized by a pronounced contraction in employment-rather than wages-concentrated among highly educated, entry-level workers in prediction-intensive occupations, with little discernible effect on aggregate employment. We argue that these patterns cannot be fully understood within existing paradigms and call for a new conceptual synthesis. By integrating task-based macroeconomic models of automation with a microeconomic view of AI as a technology that substitutes for implementation skills while complementing human judgment, we delineate the backbone of a unified framework to analyze how AI is likely to reshape job design, reallocate comparative advantage across tasks, and alter the distributional consequences of technological change. This perspective serves to structure a formal research agenda on the evolving interaction between AI and labor markets and its implications for productivity, employment, and inequality.

detail.abstract:
Marfrig Global Foods (Marfrig) CFO Tang David must decide whether to anchor new short-term and long-term contracts in US dollars. For decades, the dollar had functioned as the global safe asset, but David wondered whether headwinds on the US policy front threatened the dollar's dominance. The case offers historical context about the dollar's rise to prominence and examines the dollar's current status in relation to US tariff policy, US fiscal stability, and firm-level outcomes.This case works well as the second piece in a two-class series that covers tariffs and the US dollar; the first case is "Tariff Trouble: Navigating a Trade War in the Global Supply Chain" (UVA-GEM-0255). With the 2025 US tariffs as a backdrop, the case covers the evolving role of the US dollar as an international safe asset. Students will not only understand why the dollar holds a preeminent role in international trade and finance, but they will learn how certain shocks can imperil the dollar's position and influence global business transactions.

Excerpt

Dollars, Debt, and Destiny:Marfrig's Dilemma in a Changing Currency World

As US trade policy disrupted the world monetary system in 2025, Marfrig Global Foods (Marfrig) CFO Tang David began to rethink the Brazilian company's financial strategy. Executives were finalizing a $500 million bond issuance with a 30-year maturity and pricing a three-year international export contract, deals that the firm often completed in US dollars. Marfrig conducted business across many countries, but it regularly chose to make transactions in dollars because the US currency typically provided stability and security. The US dollar had served as the preeminent currency for global transactions for decades, but David wondered about the future of its long-held status. The value of the dollar had begun declining early that year, and the fall continued in April when the United States announced the imposition of extensive tariffs, creating uncertainty in the international sector. Aside from tariff policy, David pondered other factors that could affect the dollar's worldwide position, including the United States' growing government debt. Would the lack of clarity regarding US trade policy or the direction of US fiscal policy cause people to lose confidence in US institutions and therefore the US dollar? The weakening of the dollar might simply represent a temporary aberration, but it could also signal a more permanent shift in the global order. Was it still safe for Marfrig to anchor in US dollars?

International Monetary Systems and the Rise of the Dollar

Over time, various currencies had dominated international trade and finance. When the Republic of Florence (in what became Italy) developed into a commercial and banking hub in the 13th century, the Florentine florin (initially a gold coin and later a silver coin) became one of the first currencies to reign supreme, arising as the primary medium for large purchases across Europe and different parts of the Mediterranean region. Other currencies eventually overtook the florin as the preferred means for cross-border transactions, with the British pound gaining wide acceptance by the 19th century, when Great Britain acted as a global financial leader. The pound lost its worldwide standing after World War I (1914–18) and World War II (1939–45) ravaged Europe, while the relative strength of the US economy and US financial markets propelled the US dollar to dominant-currency status. The research utilizes primary data collected from 654 respondents, comprising 467 males and 177 females, all belonging to Generation Z.T test is used for checking significance level.The findings reveal that customer satisfaction correlates more strongly with females than males across several experiential marketing dimensions, including smell, act, sense, feel, word-of-mouth (WOM), and willingness to purchase. detail.abstract: Vaping product use has risen significantly in the United States. Health risks associated with vaping gained widespread attention in 2019 when a severe outbreak of lung injuries was linked to the use of these products. In response, Massachusetts became the first state to declare a public health emergency and enact a statewide ban on the sale of all vaping products. In this study, the authors ask an important public policy question: Does banning one vice product (vaping products) make consumers switch to a more harmful vice product in the same category (traditional cigarettes)? Using NielsenIQ retail-level sales data, the authors examine the causal impact of the ban on vaping products implemented by the state of Massachusetts. Results based on the difference-indifferences model suggest a strong spillover effect, with an increase in traditional cigarette sales following the focal ban. This increase is more pronounced for premium cigarette brands and for quick-stop retail formats. The authors propose and empirically test two different mechanisms that drive the switch: the substitution and the gateway effect. The authors find that the sales of cigarettes that share attributes with the vaping products increased following the ban and persisted after the removal of the ban, which lends evidence of substitution and gateway effects, respectively. The authors conduct a series of robustness checks to rule out alternative explanations and replicate the results from data from another state that implemented a ban on selective vaping products. The findings offer valuable insights for policymakers on the effects of regulation of vice products such as vaping products.

This research focuses on EcoDent Toothpaste Tablets, it is an innovative and eco-friendly alternative to traditional toothpaste. The study aims to explore the effectiveness, sustainability, and market potential of toothpaste tablets as a solution to plastic waste caused by conventional toothpaste tubes. By using natural and safe ingredients, EcoDent provides a convenient and environmentally responsible option for oral care. This research aims to determine whether EcoDent can succeed in the market, particularly in areas with a high concentration of dental students and professionals, such as Legarda and Recto in Manila.

The study used surveys to understand what people want and need when it comes to oral care. A total of 150 people answered questions about their habits, preferences, and knowledge of toothpaste tablets. The results showed that many people are concerned about the environment and would consider using products that reduce plastic waste. Most respondents care about effectiveness, price, ingredients, and packaging when choosing toothpaste. Although not everyone has heard of toothpaste tablets before, most are open to trying them, especially if they are affordable and offer good health benefits. title: Climate-washing Litigation: From Puffery to Material Lies

detail.title: Climate-washing Litigation: From Puffery to Material Lies

publicationDetails.detailsText: 98 University of Colorado Law Review (forthcoming 2026)

detail.abstract:
We are living in an age of information on the verge of a climate catastrophe. Access to data and increasing awareness of climate risks create consumer interest and demand for climate-friendly products and services. The use of climate-related information for advertising purposes can generate value that boost businesses’ revenue. Conversely, misinformation can also generate litigation risks at the intersection of consumer fraud, corporate accountability and environmental law. Climate-washing manifests as a distinct form of consumer fraud that targets false and misleading statements regarding climate-related risks and opportunities. The triggers for climate-washing litigation include consumer and public awareness of the climate crisis, the absence of mandatory climate-related disclosure rules and the lack of federal enforcement against climate-washing claims for consumer protection.

This Article explores the evolution, transformation and impacts of consumer fraud climate-washing lawsuits in the United States. Specifically, it analyses the principal actors that can initiate this type of litigation: (1) consumers, (2) non-profit organizations and, (3) state attorneys general. Furthermore, this Article navigates the evolution of case law and judicial interpretations that are shaping how businesses disclose climate-related information in advertising.

Public and private plaintiffs are litigating against misleading claims regarding companies' efforts to combat climate change. Climate-washing is shaping the amorphous environmental litigation landscape, by empowering consumers deceived by false or misleading climate-related representations, as a tool for the protection of the public interest and as a form of activism. Depending on the flexibility of state consumer protection statutes and their judicial interpretation, climate-washing has transformed and, arguably, expanded over time. This Article argues that climate-washing litigation is emerging as a mechanism of corporate accountability and governance that, in the absence of mandatory federal oversight and climate-related rules, is reshaping corporate disclosures, clarifying the boundary between puffery and material deception, and influencing the future regulatory landscape.

title: Training for Technology: Adoption and Productive Use of Generative AI in Legal Analysis
affiliations: The University of Hong Kong - Faculty of Law and

detail.title: Training for Technology: Adoption and Productive Use of Generative AI in Legal Analysis
detail.abstract:
Can targeted user training unlock the productive potential of generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) in professional settings? We investigate this question using a randomized study involving 164 law students completing an issue-spotting examination. Participants were assigned to one of three conditions: no GenAI access, optional access to a large language model (LLM), or optional access accompanied by an approximately ten-minute training intervention.

Training significantly increased LLM adoption—the usage rate rose from 26% to 41%—and improved examination performance. Students with trained access scored 0.27 grade points higher than those with untrained access (p = 0.027), equivalent to roughly one-third of a letter grade. By contrast, access to an LLM without training did not improve performance and was associated with shorter answers relative to no access. Using principal stratification, we decompose the overall effect into adoption and effectiveness channels. Point estimates are consistent with training operating primarily by expanding the scope of GenAI use rather than by enhancing effectiveness among existing users, though confidence intervals are wide.

Overall, our findings provide evidence that complementary investments in user training are critical for realizing GenAI productivity gains in knowledge-intensive fields where concerns about reliability may inhibit adoption.

title: Concept Capture: Linguistic Primacy and Power in Generative Knowledge Systems

detail.title: Concept Capture: Linguistic Primacy and Power in Generative Knowledge Systems
detail.abstract: Language has long been understood as a structuring force in human cognition and social organization. From Sapir and Whorf's hypothesis of linguistic relativity to Goffman's framing theory and McCombs and Shaw's agenda-setting research, scholars have demonstrated that the terms used to describe a phenomenon shape how it is perceived, evaluated, and acted upon. In traditional media environments, those who defined the language of a problem often constrained the range of acceptable solutions. In generative AI systems, this dynamic may become structurally amplified. This paper introduces the concept of Concept Capture, defined as the process by which early linguistic framing and repeated terminology shape the semantic landscape of probabilistic generative systems. Because large language models operate through token weighting, pattern recognition, and frequency reinforcement, terminology that achieves early adoption can influence not only human interpretation but also machine-generated outputs. Concept Capture extends prior theories of framing and agenda-setting into the context of generative knowledge systems, suggesting that linguistic primacy may play an increasingly decisive role in AI-era influence.

title: Institutional Noise, Strategic Deviation, and Intertemporal Collapse: A Formal Model of Agent Behaviour under Protocol Uncertainty
affiliations: University of Exeter

detail.title: Institutional Noise, Strategic Deviation, and Intertemporal Collapse: A Formal Model of Agent Behaviour under Protocol Uncertainty
detail.abstract: This paper develops a dynamic stochastic game model of strategic agent behaviour in a repeated coordination environment where the institutional rules governing payoff structures are subject to exogenous perturbation. We characterise the game as a controlled Markov chain over an evolving state space of protocol parameters, and derive volatility-adjusted Bellman equations with endogenous discount factors that respond to the variance of the institutional state process. The discount adjustment is micro-founded through a regime-survival mechanism: the probability that the institutional regime persists decreases with institutional variance via a convex hazard-rate function, so that future payoffs are conditional on regime survival rather than simply risk-adjusted. Our main results establish (i) that cooperative equilibria sustainable under fixed rules via the Folk Theorem become empty beyond a critical institutional-variance threshold (Proposition 4), (ii) that this threshold is characterised by a sharp discontinuity in the set of sustainable cooperative strategy profiles (Proposition 8), (iii) that agents rationally reallocate effort from productive activity to meta-strategic rule-influencing behaviour as variance increases (Proposition 10), and (iv) that governance instability is formally equivalent to impatience: protocol mutability endogenously compresses the effective discount factor below the cooperation threshold. Calibrated Monte Carlo simulations with 500 replications confirm the analytical predictions and locate the critical threshold within economically meaningful parameter ranges. All analytical results are numerically verified in the appendixes. The results contribute to the literature on stochastic games with regime switching, mechanism design under institutional uncertainty, and the economics of blockchain protocol governance.

detail.abstract: Despite significant progress in recent years, inadequate menstrual health and hygiene (MHH) remains a critical public health challenge in India, with approximately 30 percent of women aged 15-24 continuing to rely on cloth, rags, or nothing during menstruation. This paper examines whether delaying marriage can improve the menstrual health outcomes by estimating the causal effect of women's age at marriage on their use of period products. Using nationally representative data from India's National Family Health Survey (NFHS-5, 2019-21), we address endogeneity concerns by instrumenting age at marriage with age at menarche, a largely biologically determined factor that strongly predicts marriage timing in settings where daughters are married soon after attaining reproductive maturity. Our instrumental variable estimates reveal that delaying marriage by one year increases the probability of using period products by 7 percentage points (pp). This result is robust to alternative outcome specifications, sample restrictions, and falsification tests. We provide suggestive evidence that the effect operates through two key mechanisms: increased educational attainment and enhanced household decision-making power. Heterogeneity analysis reveals that effects are concentrated among socioeconomically disadvantaged groups, particularly women from backward castes and rural areas. These findings suggest that policies aimed at delaying child marriage, including stricter enforcement of existing laws and expansion of conditional cash transfer programs, may yield meaningful improvements in menstrual health outcomes, particularly for disadvantaged populations.

title: Transport Justice in Bristol - Rethinking Access, Equity, and Policy Impact

detail.title: Transport Justice in Bristol - Rethinking Access, Equity, and Policy Impact

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The authors declare no conflicts of interest.

All participants provided informed consent, and procedures were implemented to ensure anonymity, confidentiality, and the right to withdraw. detail.abstract:
Transport inequality in Bristol is not merely an inconvenience but a structural barrier that fundamentally shapes life chances, health outcomes, and social cohesion across the city. This research provides a comprehensive, evidence-based analysis of transport disadvantage in Bristol, combining survey data from residents, ward-level analysis across 34 areas, community engagement through town halls and focus groups, and a policy symposium with key stakeholders to develop actionable recommendations.

What we found reveals significant spatial inequality across Bristol, with Hartcliffe & Withywood showing a Transport Disadvantage Index of 85.9% whilst Stoke Bishop sits at just 21.9%, creating a 64-point gap that translates into real-world consequences: a 21.9% difference in good health outcomes and a 52.1% gap in people feeling safe after dark. Wards with worse transport also showed dramatically worse outcomes for safety, health, food security, and mental wellbeing, demonstrating how mobility constraints may compound or co-occur with other disadvantages.

Age also emerged as a critical factor, with a U-shaped pattern of difficulty across the life course. For example, the 55-64 age group reported the highest transport difficulty, with a significant difference between men and women, with women aged 55-64 facing the greatest challenges, likely reflecting health changes, caring responsibilities, and the fact that concessionary travel support doesn't begin until 65. Whilst transport difficulty is broadly similar between men and women overall, this masks important differences at specific life stages, with younger men reporting higher difficulty than younger women but pre-retirement women facing the steepest barriers of any group, and the reasons differ too because women face more safety concerns whilst men encounter more logistical barriers. Across the board, people told us that ease of travel and affordability are what make transport work or not work for them.

Through participatory research spanning town halls, focus groups, and a policy symposium, we developed a three-tier framework of recommendations spanning immediate actions like better signage and fare simplification, pilot projects testing on-demand services in transport deserts, and long-term reforms including integrated ticketing and franchise reform. Our simulations suggest comprehensive reforms could reduce the Transport Disadvantage Index gap by 50% within five years, potentially improving safety perceptions by 5.1%, and enable 12,000 additional trips weekly from people currently excluded, making clear that transport equity isn't optional for an inclusive Bristol.

title: Engines of Uplift: The Local Returns of HBCUs for Black Americans in the South, 1870-1940
affiliations: National Chung Cheng University - Department of Economics and University of Southern California

detail.title: Engines of Uplift: The Local Returns of HBCUs for Black Americans in the South, 1870-1940
detail.abstract: We study how the establishment of Historically Black Colleges and Universities (HBCUs) affected Black Americans' schooling and occupations in the postbellum South, using a newly digitized HBCU data set and full-count census data within a staggered difference-in-differences and matching framework. HBCU openings raised school enrollment among Black American youth, narrowed white-Black literacy gaps, increased occupational scores, and shifted Black workers from agriculture into higher-skilled jobs. These effects remain sizable when restricting to non-movers and accounting for population dynamics, indicating that local human capital formation, rather than selective migration, drives the long-run gains.

title: Governor Pasha’s Enemy From Within: Expulsions He Ordered From Jaffa, 1914–1917

detail.title: Governor Pasha’s Enemy From Within: Expulsions He Ordered From Jaffa, 1914–1917
detail.abstract: In the years 1914 and 1917, Ahmed Djemal Pasha, who served as the Military Governor of the Levant during World War I, expelled various groups from Jaffa, which is now part of Tel-Aviv, Israel. However, these events were notably different. In both instances, many Jews were compelled to leave the city due to suspicions of collusion with the British who had their eye on conquering that part of the Middle East. During the first expulsion, a considerable number left for the British controlled Egypt. This paper aims to explore both expulsions to understand their impact on the Jewish community in Jaffa and the wider implications for the Yishuv and Zionism during that time. The primary focus will be on the experiences of those who sought refuge in Egypt and later made their way to Israel. Through their narratives, we will investigate the lives of Jews during this tumultuous period in Jaffa, their exile in Egypt, and their eventual return to Israel or that of their descendants. The individuals highlighted are: Yechiel Michal Steinberg, his wife Simcha Ambache, and their two daughters Shoshana and Aura, Jacques Cohen (an actor), Ovadia Harari (an engineer), Albert Abraham Hemmo (a basketball player and policeman), Marcelle Ninio (a spy), and Vicki Shiran (a criminologist, sociologist, poet, film director, media personality, and activist).

title: First Law of Macroeconomics: Implications of Energy Balance Equations
affiliations: Bocconi University - Department of Finance

detail.title: First Law of Macroeconomics: Implications of Energy Balance Equations
detail.abstract: This paper introduces energy conservation - a fundamental symmetry in physical transformations - as a foundational element of production in macroeconomic models. A novel variable, Energy Differential, measures net useful energy after extraction and conversion losses. Energy balances are embedded in an endogenous-growth setting linking exogenous energy flows to technological dynamics. Net useful energy emerges as the core state variable driving output, capital formation, and innovation, endogenously giving rise to Total Factor Productivity. Energy flows shape long-run growth and business-cycle dynamics, cascading into asset prices. Empirical evidence confirms that Energy Differential is a robust driver of TFP, growth, and asset prices.

detail.abstract: This paper examines the rollback of reproductive rights in the United States as a manifestation of state power over bodily sovereignty rather than as a moral dispute over life. Situating the post-Roe v. Wade legal landscape within political philosophy, feminist ethics, and international human rights law, the analysis argues that abortion restrictions function as instruments of governance that discipline bodies, regulate gender, and reproduce structural inequality. The paper demonstrates how compelled pregnancy disproportionately burdens women, the poor, racialized communities, and those already subject to social surveillance, while reframing autonomy as conditional rather than inherent. Drawing on global ethical frameworks and comparative religious traditions, it challenges the selective use of theology and morality in state legislation, highlighting the tension between moral pluralism and imposed belief. The analysis further situates U.S. reproductive policy within a broader international context, where forced continuation of pregnancy is increasingly recognized as a violation of human rights and bodily integrity. By treating the body as a political site, the paper argues that reproductive coercion represents a broader authoritarian drift in contemporary governance, revealing how rights once grounded in privacy and autonomy can be reconstituted as privileges subject to state control. Publication Note This paper is part of an independent research series examining moral failure, state power, and ethical fracture in contemporary governance. Building on prior analyses of war, discrimination, economic violence, and historical memory, it examines reproductive control as a mechanism through which the state asserts authority over bodies and regulates social hierarchy. Drawing on political philosophy, feminist ethics, comparative religious scholarship, and international human rights law, the paper treats the post-Roe v. Wade landscape not as an isolated legal shift but as a case study in the selective recognition of autonomy and dignity. The paper is intended to function both as a standalone scholarly contribution and as a sequential chapter within a larger book-length manuscript on moral responsibility and power in 2025.

detail.abstract:
Background: Clinical artificial intelligence systems are increasingly deployed in high-stakes healthcare environments, influencing diagnosis, prognosis, treatment selection, utilization management, and population-level decision making. Although advances in machine learning have improved predictive performance in controlled settings, real-world deployments continue to exhibit silent failures, inequitable outcomes, and limited accountability. These failures often persist despite acceptable accuracy, calibration, and fairness metrics, revealing a gap between model-centric development paradigms and operational system behavior. 

Methods: This program adopts a governance-centered systems approach integrating conceptual modeling, empirical audit, formal learning theory, and systems engineering. Clinical AI is analyzed as an externally governed adaptive sociotechnical system, in which institutional, economic, regulatory, and workflow constraints shape learning dynamics, observability, and permissible actions. The program combines theoretical analysis of learning under external constraints with empirical audits of deployed clinical AI systems and the design of interoperable governance infrastructure. 

Results: Across interrelated studies, the program identifies structural failure modes that arise at deployment rather than during model training, including shortcut learning, misclassification, and inequitable behavior driven by constrained action spaces and censored feedback. Formal analysis demonstrates that externally imposed governance conditions alter learning dynamics and impose limits on auditability and adaptation that invalidate standard model-centric guarantees. Empirical audits confirm that these failures persist despite conventional validation. Infrastructure contributions demonstrate that governance and auditability can be operationalized through standards-based systems without retraining predictive models. 

Conclusions: This work reframes clinical artificial intelligence from a model-centric enterprise to a governance-centered systems discipline. By treating governance as a first-class computational object, the program provides a unified theoretical foundation, validated audit methodologies, and deployable infrastructure for accountable AI in healthcare. The framework is applicable to other high-stakes, institutionally constrained AI domains where system behavior is shaped as much by governance as by algorithmic design.

detail.abstract: Accurate semantic mapping of urban environments remains a significant challenge due to visual obstructions such as dense tree canopies and building shadows. This paper introduces a novel 5-channel AI framework, Sub-Canopy Urban Semantic Mapping, which synthesizes passive optical data with active LiDAR derivatives to achieve superior segmentation accuracy. The proposed architecture utilizes a MixVision Transformer (SegFormer) encoder integrated into a UNet decoder structure, specifically modified to ingest a pentachromatic input stack comprising RGB imagery, LiDAR surface intensity, and ground-filtered "digital deforestation" rasters.To address the inherent noise and potential data loss in multi-modal sensors, we propose a unique Exclusive Patch-Occlusion Training strategy. This method applies stochastic, multi-scale masking (80x80, 100x100, and 1300x130 patches) to diferent ratio of the training samples. Crucially, we enforce a spatial exclusivity constraint: for any given geographic coordinate, occlusion is restricted to a maximum of two out of the three data sources (RGB, Surface, or Ground), ensuring that at least one sensor provides a reliable spatial anchor at all times. Experimental results demonstrate that this 5-channel fusion approach significantly outperforms standard 3-channel RGB models, particularly in identifying sub-canopy features and delineating complex urban boundaries. The exclusive masking logic forces the model to learn robust cross-modal correlations, effectively utilizing sensor redundancy to mitigate the impact of shadows and sensor-specific occlusions. This research provides a scalable and resilient methodology for high-fidelity urban land-cover classification using heterogeneous remote sensing data.

detail.abstract: This paper investigates the impact of skin tone on political outcomes by introducing a novel method for measuring skin color through machine learning techniques. Using this approach, we extract the skin tones of all candidates in Brazilian elections from 2016 to 2022. Our methodology offers advantages over self-reported racial classifications, as 25% of politicians running in multiple elections change their selfdeclared race, indicating substantial bias and endogeneity. Our findings suggest that relying solely on self-declared race underestimates the influence of race in politics. Employing a regression discontinuity design in tight interracial elections, we find no significant difference in skin tone between self-declared white and non-white candidates. Additionally, we observe shifts in campaign spending patterns: dark-skinned candidates spent less than lighter-skinned candidates in 2016, but this trend reversed in 2020. In municipalities where darker-skinned mayors won tightly contested elections, the average income of mixed-race voters was higher. However, once in office, dark-skinned mayors appointed 25 percentage points fewer self-declared non-white and 12 percentage points fewer self-declared Black cabinet members compared to their lighter-skinned counterparts. Lastly, we find evidence of a role model effect, where the election of darker-skinned mayors positively influenced Black student outcomes before the COVID-19 pandemic. These effects are either muted or reversed for self-declared white and non-white mayors in closely contested elections. Our results highlight the complexities of race, representation, and electoral dynamics, calling for a reassessment of studies that rely solely on self-reported racial identity.

detail.abstract:
In recent years, as concerns about artificial intelligence (AI) have grown, the federal government has taken steps to eliminate the few AI regulations that once existed. This deregulatory turn comes as a growing chorus of Nobel Prize winners and a majority of surveyed AI experts are warning of a significant risk of AI causing human extinction. Although skeptics remain and the debate continues, concerns about AI’s existential risks have gone mainstream. This Article brings consideration of these risks into the mainstream of legal scholarship. It offers the most comprehensive treatment in legal scholarship of the debate surrounding existential risks posed by advanced AI systems.

We classify and analyze existential AI risks in three categories: human-directed risks, accident risks, and loss-of-control risks. The goal is to make these risks legible to legal institutions that must make regulatory choices under uncertainty. Drawing on, and contributing to, the substantial literature on regulation under uncertainty, this Article argues that policymakers should address existential AI risks with adaptive regulation that preserves optionality for the future. This flexible approach reflects the uncertain future path of AI and the potentially enormous magnitude of its harms, even when weighed against its potentially remarkable upsides. In calling for regulation, we also critique and deconstruct the metaphor of the ‘AI arms race,’ which drives much of the current deregulatory push.

The Article closes by offering, for the first time, a set of concrete regulatory solutions for addressing existential AI risk. We do not seek to end the ongoing debate about AI’s risks. But we do marshal evidence to show that existential AI risks are worthy of a policy response, similar to any other non-trivial catastrophic risk.

detail.abstract: This study analyzes food price variations between the Brazilian capitals of São Paulo and Curitiba during the fourth quarter of 2025. Using data from the Extended National Consumer Price Index (IPCA-E), the research employs percentage difference and relative price elasticity calculations to understand local inflation dynamics. The results reveal a significant decoupling in food price behavior: while São Paulo experienced a cumulative increase of 0.25% in food costs, Curitiba recorded a deflationary trend of -0.32% in the same sector, despite an overall positive inflation rate of 0.21%. The analysis suggests that regional fiscal policies, specifically the state of Paraná's exemption of ICMS on 21 basic food basket items, effectively neutralized broader inflationary pressures. Conversely, higher per capita income in São Paulo sustained demand and price increases despite a lower nominal tax rate. The findings emphasize that local factors, such as state tax structures and income levels, are crucial for accurately interpreting essential goods' price movements beyond national indicators.

detail.abstract:
Ensuring legislative accountability in multi-party systems requires quantitative tools that reveal actual voting behavior beyond formal party affiliations. We present a network- based framework for analyzing parliamentary dynamics at multiple scales, capturing coalition structure, group coherence, and individual influence. Applied to over 4 million vote expressions from the Italian Parliament across three government formations (2018- 2021), the methodology combines network modularity, voting distance metrics, and betweenness centrality to map the structure of collective decision-making.

Using this framework, we show that system-level polarization, as captured by network modularity, varies systematically with coalition structure rather than coalition size. Technical governments display paradoxically lower global polarization despite broader formal support, reflecting structurally mixed voting patterns rather than unified blocs. On polarizing issues such as immigration, network polarization depends strongly on the fragmentation or cohesion of the opposition, even when the governing coalition votes cohesively. Betweenness analysis reveals that mediator roles are highly concentrated, with only about 2% of parliamentarians acting as structural bridges between communities. Community detection further uncovers implicit coalitions that are not apparent from declared alliances.

The framework relies exclusively on public roll-call data, enabling reproducible analysis and direct applicability to any legislature with transparent voting records. By linking individual voting behavior to emergent system-level structure, the methodology provides quantitative infrastructure for comparative analysis of legislative voting networks and coalition monitoring, enabling systematic assessment of legislative behaviour.

detail.abstract:
This report investigates how different voting systems affect decision-making within SingularityNET’s Deep Funding program, particularly focusing on addressing concerns about fairness, community engagement, and optimal resource allocation. One key finding is that SingularityNET’s Deep Fund program is not currently operating as a fully decentralized ecosystem, with one wallet holding 86% of the voters' AGIX tokens and 1.75% of the AGIX circulation supply. Applying the square root to the wallets to compute voting credits, the largest wallet has 34% of the voting credits, which is sufficient to retain disproportionate influence over the outcomes. Additionally, considering non-zero wallets who voted, 3% of wallets have 52% of the voting credits and 19% of the wallets have 90% of the voting credits. Further investigation is needed to understand how this centralization occurred and its implications for governance.

Despite this concern, simulation results provide preliminary evidence that Preferential Quadratic Voting (PQV) could significantly improve decision-making, leading to higher average community welfare and thus more efficient outcomes. The phase preferential quadratic voting is used to emphasize the voters ability to express the strength of their preference and to contrast with applying the square-root to the wallet holdings but is functionally just the QV method. Based on these findings, we recommend conducting a beta round in which the current 1-10 ranking system is replaced with preference weighting using quadratic voting, allowing for more effective outcomes in decision-making in the funding process.

detail.abstract:
Suicide research has traditionally relied on additive risk factor models in which crisis is treated as the cumulative accumulation of static vulnerabilities. Although numerous biological, psychological and social correlates have been identified, prospective prediction of suicidal behavior remains modest. This persistent limitation suggests structural constraints within linear aggregation frameworks rather than simple data insufficiency.

The Talk Hope Integrated Model (THIM) proposes a five-variable dynamical architecture in which adolescent crisis is conceptualized as a state transition. The system consists of total load A(t), accumulated fatigue F(t), baseline structural inertia Ω, operational buffer β(t) and visibility Φ(t). Fatigue evolves as a visibility-modulated leaky integral of load, while effective structural resistance declines through fatigue-dependent erosion.

Instability is defined through a pressure–resistance inequality: collapse occurs when instantaneous load acceleration exceeds total effective defense, represented by fatigue-modulated structural inertia plus accessible operational buffering. This formulation encodes state memory, signal distortion and endogenous threshold drift within a bounded dynamical system. The model predicts hysteresis, such that reduction of external load does not immediately restore stability because accumulated fatigue suppresses effective resistance over time.

For field application, internal state variables are mapped onto a four-indicator Shadow Protocol consisting of withdrawal, behavioral contrast, discordant affect and anchor presence, enabling structured longitudinal monitoring. The framework is explicitly falsifiable and parameter-bounded. It does not claim deterministic prediction of individual outcomes but offers a testable dynamical structure for examining instability trajectories in adolescent suicide prevention research.

detail.abstract: The COVID-19 pandemic triggered a global disruption to international trade, creating a rare opportunity for empirically examining economic resilience under a large-scale shock. The rebound of international trade after the initial lockdown is often seen as evidence of systemic resilience, yet this recovery also coincided with a resurgence in global CO2 emissions. This response to systemic stress raises key questions for sustainability scholars: under what conditions does resilience in global trade reproduce environmentally unsustainable outcomes, and how can a resilience analysis help inform transformative interventions aimed towards greater sustainability? Building on social-ecological resilience theory, this study conceptualizes resilience as encompassing shock absorption, rebound, adaptive reorganization, and the potential for transformation. We apply this framework to embodied carbon trade flows across 164 countries and 120 sectors from 2019 to 2021. Using a combination  Social Network Analysis (SNA) and Structural Decomposition Analysis (SDA) our results indicate how the embodied carbon trade network absorbed the COVID-19 shock and rebounded to pre-pandemic network patterns, with only limited and short-term adaptive reorganization. We further demonstrate that the rebound in global emissions was driven primarily by renewed growth in final demand and the reactivation of carbon-intensive supply chains. Reflecting on these results, our study identifies leverage points for transformative intervention at both the structural (network) and economic-driver levels. These include demand-side change in major consuming economies and the governance of trade reconfiguration during recovery phases, thus highlighting potential pathways that would better align trade resilience with long-term sustainability goals.

detail.abstract: The weakening of the regional economy is often a complex social problem. Criminal behavior can occur, such as the theft of residents’ houses, caused by the weakening of the regional economy. The study was conducted in Merangin Regency, Jambi Province, the second-largest palm oilproducing province after Riau Province. Merangin is a district with the largest palm oil productivity in Jambi Province. Merangin Regency’s dependence on palm oil production is the reason why this location is suitable for research. This is caused by the loss of people’s fixed income and the influence of other factors, such as drug consumption, which requires perpetrators to fulfill their needs by stealing. The weakening of the local economy also causes low microeconomic resilience because the fulfillment of household needs and income are reduced. Meanwhile, national security, which is a function of the police institution, is also disrupted because negative assumptions about the police are developing in society, resulting in feelings of reluctance and fear of reporting to the police if a criminal act of theft occurs in the Merangin Regency.

detail.abstract: Policymakers around the world are introducing legislation seeking to encourage the local production of key inputs to reduce risks from excessive dependencies on foreign suppliers. We utilise a global dynamic general equilibrium model to analyse the macroeconomic effects of supply chain reorientation through localisation policies, such as reshoring and friendshoring production, via a novel non-tariff mechanism. Focusing on the euro area, we find that localisation policies are inflationary, imply transition costs and generally have a negative long-run effect on aggregate domestic output. Untargeted localisation policies do not necessarily improve macroeconomic resilience against shocks that proxy supply chain disruptions. Sensitivity to regional shocks increases, while resilience to global shocks is unaffected. We provide some recommendations for policymakers considering implementing a localisation agenda.
