detail.abstract: Artificial intelligence viewed through a lens as a skill-biased technological innovation, with a special attention toward labor markets and productivity growth. Rather than AI being an unprecedented disruption, the analysis of the effects of it in real world situations situates recent developments within established economic frameworks related to automation and task substitution. Publicly available labor market and productivity data suggest AI adoption generates different effects across different occupations, complementing higher-skill labor while simultaneously increasing adjustment pressures with routine tasks. While productivity gains associated with AI may support long term economic growth, short-run labor market disruptions raise concerns regarding wage inequality and workforce adaptation. These dynamics underscore the importance of education, reskilling, and institutional responses in shaping the economic outcomes of artificial intelligence. 1. Introduction-Artificial intelligence has become increasingly common across many parts of the economy, changing how work is done and how firms produce output. AI tools are now used.

title: Underbetting and Accounting Conservatism
affiliations: and Columbia University - Columbia Business School, Accounting, Business Law & Taxation

detail.title: Underbetting and Accounting Conservatism

declarations.declarationOfInterest: No conflicts
declarations.ethicsApproval: NA
declarations.funderStatement: None

detail.abstract: Information is what the user makes of it and different users will reach different probabilities from the same information. We consider how "naive" users, who overstate the firm's probability of success, inflate the asset price and harm both themselves and market efficiency by pricing "sophisticated" investors out of the market. Surprising results reveal how all investors benefit by "underbetting their beliefs" or betting as if they are more risk averse than they are. Drawing on models of underbetting developed by mathematicians, we explain how investors who accept that their probabilities are error prone react by investing conservatively, as if they discount indications that seem to warrant a larger "bet". While not raised in accounting theory, traditional accounting conservatism can induce underbetting with the same benefits that gamblers find, generally more so because the share price is lower in a more prudent or risk averse market.

title: Good Faith as Integrity: Good Faith and the Nature of Voluntary Obligation
affiliations: Notre Dame Law School

detail.title: Good Faith as Integrity: Good Faith and the Nature of Voluntary Obligation

publicationDetails.detailsText: Theoretical Inquiries in Law (forthcoming)

detail.abstract: Good faith is a protean concept: it takes on different shades of meaning, and has been made to do many quite distinctive things, in private, public, and international law. These qualities have made good faith perplexing. Partly in consequence, conventional wisdom on good faith is decidedly anti-theoretical. Some have argued that good faith is indefinable. Others argue that the law knows no concept of good faith: reference to good faith is just a placeholder for its antonym, bad faith. In this essay, I suggest that the conventional wisdom is wrong. One can extract a coherent, generalizable, notion of good faith from the law. On the theory presented here, illustrated in respect of voluntary obligations, good faith consists in personal integrity with respect to juridical speech acts. To evince good faith in this sense is to demonstrate fidelity to the known legal significance (objective legal meaning) of one's speech acts and attendant jural relations. A person who acts in good faith behaves righteously in a specifically legal sense. Bad faith, correlatively, involves lack of integrity: iniquity. Iniquity implies a defect in one's deliberate behavior, and hence goes to character, consistent with the intuition that bad faith is morally culpable. But bad faith in law has distinctively legal upshots: it threatens to undermine the institutional integrity of law. Thus, good faith is properly considered an über-norm of foundational importance to law and to legality.

title: Separation of Powers or Division of Labor? Patent Interference Disputes, the Grand Narrative, and the History of the Administrative State, 1790-1940
affiliations: and University of Michigan Law School

detail.title: Separation of Powers or Division of Labor? Patent Interference Disputes, the Grand Narrative, and the History of the Administrative State, 1790-1940

declarations.declarationOfInterest: none
declarations.funderStatement: University of Michigan Law School

detail.abstract: We use the history of the Patent Office to challenge the Grand Narrative of separation of powers that the current Supreme Court is using to invalidate congressional designs for administrative agencies.  Focusing on the adjudication of patent interference disputes—cases in which two or more inventors applied for patents for essentially the same technology—we find that the division of labor between the Patent Office and the courts shifted repeatedly and dramatically over the century and a half preceding the Administrative Procedure Act.  Rather than worries about separation of powers, the main drivers of change were (1) the Patent Office’s efforts to curb inventors’ exploitation of interference procedures to delay the award of patents to rivals and (2) the need to manage the workload that interference appeals imposed on the overburdened Patent Office and courts.  Innovations in Patent Office procedures led to dramatic improvements in the efficiency of its frontline adjudication of interferences, but officials found it much more difficult to prevent losing parties from abusing appeals opportunistically.  At the behest of the Patent Office, Congress repeatedly revised the appeals process for interferences, trying out direct review by ad hoc arbitration panels, individual judges, and variously constituted courts.  It even eliminated direct appeals of interference decisions from 1870 until 1893, while continuing to provide for appeals from rejections of patent applications (where opportunistic delays posed less serious problems).  Although interference parties sometimes raised legal challenges to these review structures, they reached a dead end in the Supreme Court, which throughout the nineteenth century deferred to Congress’s authority to design the system.  Finally, in 1939, after a century of trial and error, the Patent Office convinced Congress to eliminate all internal appeals in interference cases within the Patent Office, to authorize the Patent Office to issue patents based on its frontline adjudications of priority, and to shift review of interference decisions entirely to the courts.  Again, this change did not apply to rejections of patent applications, which were still reviewed internally before they could be appealed to the courts. Both the great variety of appeal structures enacted over the years and the repeated divergence in the treatment of appeals of interferences and rejections support our emphasis on the primary role that pragmatic concerns played in the evolving division of labor between the Patent Office and the courts.  This history reveals flexible adaptation over time rather than conformity to a standard model of separation of powers traceable to the framers.

title: Geotime (TG_BASE): A Trade-Secret-Safe Event-Time Transformation that Systematically Improves Normality Diagnostics Across Seven Futures Asset Classes

detail.title: Geotime (TG_BASE): A Trade-Secret-Safe Event-Time Transformation that Systematically Improves Normality Diagnostics Across Seven Futures Asset Classes

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author is the founder and CEO of Geotime-Helios, Inc., which holds proprietary rights to the TG_BASE transformation described in this paper.
declarations.ethicsApproval: Not applicable. This study uses publicly available market data and does not involve human subjects.
declarations.funderStatement: This research was self-funded by Geotime-Helios, Inc.

detail.abstract: Financial returns particularly at high frequency are famously non-Gaussian, with heavy tails and persistent volatility dynamics that complicate risk measurement and statistical modeling (Mandelbrot, 1963; Cont, 2001; Engle, 1982; Bollerslev, 1986). This paper studies TG_BASE, an event-time transformation defined by observable properties (its implementation is proprietary): it replaces a fixed ∆t clock with an operational index built from causally detected geometric pivots that are confirmed with a finite delay to prevent repainting. The motivation comes from the broad time-change perspective in stochastic process theory, including the DambisDubinsSchwarz theorem and the operationaltime/subordination literature (Dambis, 1965; Dubins and Schwarz, 1965; Mandelbrot and Taylor, 1967; Clark, 1973; Ané and Geman, 2000). We propose an auditable evaluation protocol with two baselines standard clock-time returns, and clock-time returns sampled at event timestamps and a six-metric gate based on excess kurtosis, 3σ and 5σ tail exceedance rates, the Hill tail index (Hill, 1975), a volatility-dependence diagnostic, and a fair-matched outlier control. Experiments are conducted on 28 continuous instruments spanning FX, equity indices, energy, metals, rates, agriculture, and crypto futures, and on a 196-point symbol × timeframe grid. At the causal (base-sampling) layer, 24 of 28 symbols (85.7%) satisfy the gate, and 18 of 28 (64.3%) remain acceptable under robustness stress tests and adversarial integrity checks. We release derived tables, data manifests, and audit artifacts suffcient to verify reported aggregates, while withholding detector parameterization and event-definition thresholds. Cross-symbol aggregates are computed on a canonical overlap window (the intersection of data availability across symbols). Audit-ready reproducibility artifacts (data manifests, derived tables, and integrity summaries) are available in a public repository referenced in Section 9.

title: First-Mover Advantage in Funds Revisited
affiliations: and

detail.title: First-Mover Advantage in Funds Revisited

publicationDetails.detailsText: Central Bank of Ireland Research Paper Series Vol. 2024, No. 6
publicationDetails.journalName: Central Bank of Ireland Research Paper Series

detail.abstract: We investigate the first-mover advantage that motivates occasional run-like redemptions from mutual funds with liquidity mismatches. The role of such behavior in amplifying financial crises and the necessity for its regulation remain subjects of ongoing debate. This paper examines the presence and impact of first-mover advantage flows using detailed data from a substantial cohort of EU-regulated funds. We confirm that corporate bond funds, unlike equity funds, exhibit a concave flow-to-performance relationship, with the outflow response to poor performance being more pronounced than the inflow response to good performance. During the exogenous shock in March 2020, corporate bond funds with prone-to-run characteristics, despite not holding more illiquid assets, experienced significantly larger increases in net outflows. These patterns align with greater strategic complementarities in corporate bond funds and indicate a fragility concern. Furthermore, after controlling for asset liquidity and several other asset characteristics, as well as time-varying fundamental information, bonds and equities with larger ownership exposure to prone-to-run funds suffered greater price impacts. The findings collectively support the existence of strategic complementarities arising from mutual fund structures and demonstrate how the resulting redemption behaviour can amplify crisis dynamics.

title: Administrative Meets Survey Data: Measuring Household Indebtedness in Ireland
affiliations: and Central Bank of Ireland

detail.title: Administrative Meets Survey Data: Measuring Household Indebtedness in Ireland

publicationDetails.detailsText: Central Bank of Ireland Research Paper Series No. 2, 2024
publicationDetails.journalName: Central Bank of Ireland Research Paper Series

detail.abstract: The 2020 Household Finance and Consumption Survey (HFCS) marked the first time that survey data from Irish households was supplemented with administrative data from the Central Bank’s Central Credit Register (CCR). Using household level data from the panel component of the survey, weighted to the full population in 2018, we develop a simple approach for estimating measurement error and applying it, find at least one third of households hold “revealed debt” worth almost 13 per cent of the value of total debt outstanding in 2020. Revealed debt is debt which was previously not reported in the HFCS but has come to light with the inclusion of the CCR. In doing so, we show that incorporating the CCR into the HFCS has helped to correct for under-reporting and improved the overall quality of liabilities data in the survey. Controlling for demographic and income characteristics, we find that households with more complex balance sheets are more likely to hold revealed debt. The results suggest that incorporating administrative data into surveys can help alleviate issues surrounding recall bias and other human errors that may generate initial misreporting.

title: Owner-Occupied Housing Costs, Policy Communication, and Inflation Expectations

detail.title: Owner-Occupied Housing Costs, Policy Communication, and Inflation Expectations

publicationDetails.detailsText: Central Bank of Ireland Research Paper Series No. 3, 2024
publicationDetails.journalName: Central Bank of Ireland Research Paper Series

detail.abstract: The ECB concluded its strategy review in 2021 with a plan to include owner-occupied housing (OOH) costs in its inflation measure in the future. This paper uses the Bundesbank's online household panel to study how household expectations would react to this change. We conducted a survey experiment with different information treatments and compared long-run expectations for euro area overall inflation, interest rates, and OOH inflation. Long-run expectations are typically higher for OOH inflation than overall inflation, and both are unanchored from the ECB's target at the time of the survey. We find significantly higher inflation expectations under the treatment where OOH costs are assumed to be fully included in the inflation measure. This information effect is heterogeneous as, among others, homeowners and respondents with low trust in the ECB react more strongly. However, inflation expectations remain stable when information about past OOH inflation is also given. Careful communication design could thus prevent expectations from becoming more de-anchored.

title: Institutional Investment and Residential Rental Market Dynamics

publicationDetails.detailsText: Central Bank of Ireland Research Paper Series No. 1, 2024

detail.abstract: The impact of institutional investment on residential rental markets is a topic that draws much attention, but for which limited evidence exists. This paper aims to remedy this by analysing the direct and indirect impact of institutional investment in existing housing stock on residential rents at the property level, using Ireland as a case study. Ireland is particularly suited, as large portfolios of rental properties became available for purchase due to the Global Financial Crisis (GFC), enticing institutional investors into Ireland's rental market for the first time. By focusing on investment in existing stock, the analysis isolates the impact of institutional investment from the effect it can have on local rental markets when it is channelled to new rental housing-a supply effect which should reduce rents. The study finds that institutional investors increased the level of rents by 4.1 percentage points more than other landlords with comparable properties following purchase. Available evidence supports many different causal mechanisms, including bargaining power, institutional landlords providing a higher cost-higher quality service, and institutional landlords placing greater emphasis on profitability.

title: To be, or not to be paid - reasoning about financial compensation and motivation in relation to study participation - a qualitative analysis
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN, affiliation not provided to SSRN, affiliation not provided to SSRN, University of Pennsylvania School of Nursing and affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: To be, or not to be paid - reasoning about financial compensation and motivation in relation to study participation - a qualitative analysis
detail.abstract: Introduction: The practice of compensating individuals for participation in clinical research varies significantly across countries. Purpose: This study explores perceptions of financial compensation for participating in research studies. Methods: Data was collected within a multicentre, randomized, controlled trial evaluating the effects of tele-yoga. Semi-structured telephone interviews were conducted between March 2022 and April 2023 with 35 participants diagnosed with heart failure from two hospitals in Sweden. Result: Thematic analysis revealed three main themes: Participation with altruistic motives, Participation brings personal benefits, and Financial compensation can impact study quality. Participants predominantly viewed financial compensation negatively, emphasizing altruistic motives such as contributing to scientific knowledge and fulfilling a duty to society. Personal benefits, including potential health improvements and enhanced interaction with healthcare professionals, were also significant motivators. Financial compensation for expenses was seen as beneficial for facilitating recruitment and increasing engagement. However, ethical concerns were raised about the potential for financial incentives to undermine the voluntary nature of participation and affect the integrity of the study. Conclusion: The study highlights that altruistic and personal motives are stronger motivators than financial compensation, which points out the need for clearer guidelines and a standardized approach to ensure ethical compensation practices. Researchers should balance ethical principles with practical considerations to design studies that enhance participant experience and satisfaction, leading to higher quality data and more reliable results.Keywords: Patient Participation,  Reimbursement Mechanisms,  Motivation, Attitudes, Qualitative research.  What is already known Financial compensation practices differ globally. It is mandatory to adhere to organizational or local guidelines for compensating community members and covering travel expenses.The topic of financial compensation for participants in research is an issue that has been discussed with some studies exploring its ethical, practical, and regulatory aspects.Different ethical, legal, and policy guidelines on payment to participants when performing international studies can be a challenging.   What this paper adds In-depth insights into what motivates participants in an interventional study to participate in clinical research.Participants described that research participation should be motivated by altruistic motives, such as contributing to new knowledge as well as personal benefits. Financial compensation was generally viewed as less important.While compensation may increase participation, especially among individuals with lower socioeconomic status, participants expressed concerns about how payment could affect voluntariness.

title: Regime-Dependent Spillovers and Network Dynamics of ESG Assets
affiliations: Guangdong University of Foreign Studies, Guangdong University of Foreign Studies and Asia University, Department of Finance

detail.title: Regime-Dependent Spillovers and Network Dynamics of ESG Assets

publicationDetails.detailsText: FINANA-D-26-00357

detail.abstract: This study examines the systemic role and cross-market risk transmission of ESG assets across different market regimes. A partial correlation–based net dependence network, minimum spanning tree (MST), and time-varying parameter VAR model with generalized forecast error variance decomposition (GFEVD) are employed to jointly capture static structures and dynamic spillovers. Using data from the pre-crisis, COVID-19, and Russia–Ukraine conflict periods, the results show that total connectedness rises sharply and remains elevated during both crises, with return spillovers exhibiting stronger surges than volatility spillovers, reflecting the persistence of risk expectations. The World Sustainability Index and Islamic Stocks consistently act as core transmitters, while the S&P 500 and North America Sustainability Index function as intermediaries. Conversely, the Emerging Market Sustainability Index, gold, Bitcoin, oil, and Sukuk are net receivers. The Green Bond Index smooths return variances and serves as a bridge rather than a driver. The bridging role shifts across regimes—EMarket and Sukuk dominate during the pandemic, while SPGB and the Eurozone index lead during the Russia–Ukraine conflict—linking ESG cores with conventional assets. Crisis-induced network densification and bridging reconfiguration jointly compressed diversification space. Mechanistically, regime shifts and multi-factor segmentation rotate factor weights and inter-block couplings, triggering shortest-path rerouting reinforced by policy-driven capital flows. Overall, the study provides structural and dynamic evidence on ESG assets’ stability and transmission mechanisms, offering implications for portfolio rebalancing and systemic risk management.

title: Who Gets Jobs Matters: Monetary Policy and the Labour Market in HANK and SAM
affiliations: Aix-Marseille University - Aix-Marseille School of Economics and

detail.title: Who Gets Jobs Matters: Monetary Policy and the Labour Market in HANK and SAM

publicationDetails.detailsText: Central Bank of Ireland Research Paper Series No. 10, 2023
publicationDetails.journalName: Central Bank of Ireland Research Paper Series

detail.abstract: This paper first provides empirical evidence that labour market outcomes for the less educated, who also tend to be poorer, are substantially more volatile than those for the well-educated, who tend to be richer. We estimate job finding rates and separation rates by educational attainment for several European countries and find that job finding rates are smaller and separation rates larger at lower educational attainment levels. At cyclical frequencies, fluctuations of the job finding rate explain up to 80% of unemployment fluctuations for the less educated. We then construct a stylised HANK model augmented with search and matching and ex-ante heterogeneity in terms of educational attainment. We show that monetary policy has stronger effects when the job market for the less educated and, hence, poorer is more volatile. The reason is that these workers have the most procyclical income coupled with the highest marginal propensity to consume. An expansionary monetary policy shock that increases labour demand disproportionally affects the labour market segment for the less educated, causing a strong increase in consumption. This further amplifies labour demand and increases labour income of the poor even more, amplifying the initial effect. The same mechanism carries over to forward guidance.

title: A Fuzzy Hybrid Decision Support System (DSS) to Govern Non-linear Dynamics and Uncertainty in AI-Augmented Software Development
affiliations: Valahia University of Targoviste, Valahia University of Targoviste,  and

detail.title: A Fuzzy Hybrid Decision Support System (DSS) to Govern Non-linear Dynamics and Uncertainty in AI-Augmented Software Development

publicationDetails.detailsText: COMIND-D-26-00371

detail.abstract: The rapid integration of Large Language Models into the Software Development Life Cycle has given rise to an AI Productivity Paradox, characterized by a structural gap between individual developer speed and aggregate organizational delivery performance. While established frameworks like DORA and SPACE focus on monitoring system health, delivery stability, and multidimensional productivity constructs, they often lack the prescriptive capacity to govern the non-linear dynamics and epistemic uncertainty inherent to AI-mediated work. The main contribution of this paper is the development of a novel Fuzzy Hybrid Decision Support System (DSS) that pivots toward an uncertainty-aware governance model, which is specifically designed to handle the noise and structural ambiguity of AI-assisted engineering.  Instead of treating metrics as exact or infallible numbers, this approach uses fuzzy logic to translate complex technical signals into clear, risk-based assessments, helping leaders identify hidden work bottlenecks and quality issues even when data is noisy or incomplete. By operationalizing three specialized constructs, including Delivered Story Points per Deployment (DSPD) to audit value density, Lead Time for Business Features (LTBF) to identify flow constraints in requirements phases often overlooked by standard lead time metrics, and the Acceptance/Churn Duo to predict technical debt, this framework moves beyond measuring mere volume. The study embeds fuzzy logic as the principal inferential mechanism, allowing leaders to manage systemic pathologies such as thrashing and verification saturation by mapping low-level telemetry into high-level probabilistic performance states. The framework introduces a novel socio-technical governance mechanism that utilizes fuzzy logic to formally address the AI-driven development.

title: Criminal Records, the Right to be Forgotten, and Inclusive Insurance: Risk, Rehabilitation, and Data Governance in Underwriting
affiliations: Université du Québec à Montréal and David Schraub Actuarial Consultancy

detail.title: Criminal Records, the Right to be Forgotten, and Inclusive Insurance: Risk, Rehabilitation, and Data Governance in Underwriting
detail.abstract: Criminal history information (CHx) is increasingly used in insurance screening and underwriting, yet it remains under-theorized in the inclusive insurance literature despite its potential to widen protection gaps through quote-gating, opaque third-party data pipelines, and limited avenues for correction. This article argues that criminalhistory underwriting is a joint problem of risk governance and information governance. Criminal justice information is time-sensitive and legally structured, but automated decision systems and vendor supply chains can operationalize it as durable stigma, particularly when records persist across brokers, archives, and derivative products that fail to reflect status changes such as sealing, expungement, or spentness. The article maps where CHx can enter the insurance lifecycle (pre-quote funnels, underwriting/pricing, claims and renewal) and identifies inclusion-relevant failure modes linked to provenance, data quality, update lag, and weak procedural safeguards. It then develops a conceptual framework distinguishing defensible risk relevance from digital punishment, and translates that framework into implementable mechanisms for more inclusive practice: redemption-by-design (time windows and decaying weights), data minimization and purpose limitation grounded in marginal predictive value, auditable vendor governance, and due-process safeguards providing actionable notice, explanation, and rapid correction. The article concludes with a governance standard for regulators and insurers: the key question is not whether CHx is used, but whether any use is demonstrably incremental, time-bounded, contestable, and governable across the data supply chain.

title: GDP, A Poor Indicator of Overall Wellbeing of a Nation: A Case Study of Pakistans Overall Progress
affiliations: Iqra University Karachi

detail.title: GDP, A Poor Indicator of Overall Wellbeing of a Nation: A Case Study of Pakistans Overall Progress
detail.abstract: The gross domestic product is widely known for the measurement of the wellbeing of any particular nation and its economic progress. It gained wide acceptance from 1990's as a valuable indicator of a nation's overall development and progress. On the other hand, GDP has its flaws to accurately measure any nation's wealth. Additionally, to keep up with the GDP most of the countries are polluting their environments for industrial development, refraining their people from public services. Therefore, a country building nuclear weapons, and another country building hospitals, can both be accounted equal as far as the GDP is concerned. It has been indicated by an inclusive wealth report 2018 that almost 44 out of the 140 countries in the world are not on their sustainable path but progressing well according to GDP. On the other hand, for the measure of wellbeing of any nation, inclusive wealth could be a good indicator. Inclusive wealth accounts to prospects like; management capital, human capital and also the natural capital of a particular country. In this particular research, Pakistan's inclusive wealth will be analysed against its GDP through secondary data collection that will be mostly taken from the statistics that are available on the online forums and through the various reports of UN and world economic forum.

title: Tanneries, Pollution, and Water Quality in the Ganges in Kanpur, India: A Stochastic Analysis
affiliations: Rochester Institute of Technology and University of Texas at San Antonio - College of Business - Department of Economics

detail.title: Tanneries, Pollution, and Water Quality in the Ganges in Kanpur, India: A Stochastic Analysis

contentType.other: Unpublished paper under review for publication.

detail.abstract: Water quality in the Ganges River in Kanpur, India, is the result of two opposite factors. The positive factor arises from the regulations that compel tanneries to treat their wastewater before this water is discharged into the Ganges. The negative factor stems from cheating, bribery, and non-compliance by some tanneries which leads to the dumping of insufficiently treated wastewater into the Ganges. We shed light on two goals by analyzing a stochastic model of Ganges water quality that is the outcome of the above two factors. Our first goal is to study the probabilistic evolution of water quality in the Ganges and to then compute the likelihood that water quality will improve to an exogenously specified level denoted by 𝑄. Our second goal is to ascertain the expected amount of time it will take for water quality to get to this level 𝑄 and to then discuss related issues.

title: Pricing Climate Risk: Hurricane Models and Home Insurance Over the Last Two Decades
affiliations: University of California, San Diego (UCSD) - Department of Economics, Florida State University, University of Wisconsin-Madison and University of Georgia - Department of Insurance, Legal Studies, Real Estate

detail.title: Pricing Climate Risk: Hurricane Models and Home Insurance Over the Last Two Decades
detail.abstract: To what extent do rising homeowners insurance premiums reflect growing climate risk? We examine hurricane risk in Florida and how insurers price it. Insurers rely on proprietary, third-party catastrophe models that estimate property-level expected losses. Using data from these models, we describe estimated hurricane risk across the state and how it evolved from 2006 to 2023. Expected property losses from hurricanes increased by 50%. Turning to insurance prices, we collect the premium rate filing data for insurers representing 70% of the total market. Insurers wanting to adjust their hurricane premium rates must file a request with the state regulator and justify the change with hurricane model output. Leveraging discrete updates to hurricane models, we estimate that a $1 increase in expected losses increases hurricane premiums by $5.82. Overall, hurricane premiums increased by more than 200% during our period of study. We consider potential mechanisms and find that the large markup above expected loss appears to reflect 1) reliance in the insurance market on local, limitedly diversified insurers, paired with 2) the rising cost of reinsurance.

title: Informal Labor Market, Inflation and Monetary Policy
affiliations: University of Milano

detail.title: Informal Labor Market, Inflation and Monetary Policy

publicationDetails.detailsText: University of Milan Bicocca Department of Economics, Management and Statistics Working Paper No. 569
publicationDetails.journalName: University of Milan Bicocca Department of Economics, Management & Statistics Research Paper Series

detail.abstract: Informality represents a pervasive feature of many emerging and developing economies, yet standard macroeconomic models often ignore its effects, potentially biasing the analysis of shocks and the design of monetary policy. This paper studies the macroeconomic and policy implications of informality using a structural VAR for Colombia and a twoagent New Keynesian model with formal and informal sectors, featuring heterogeneous households including hand-to-mouth consumers. I show that informal labor supply shocks generate sectoral reallocation: informal activity absorbs part of the shock, sustaining aggregate output while altering wages, hours, and capital allocation. In contrast, monetary policy shocks propagate more strongly when informality is present, amplifying distributional and capital-reallocation effects. Critically, the presence of informality alters equilibrium determinacy: standard Taylor rules may fail to ensure uniqueness, with stability depending on the share of Ricardian households, the size of the informal sector, and the monetary policy stance. My findings highlight that accounting for informal production is essential for understanding transmission mechanisms and designing effective policy in economies with significant informality.

title: NEOS - A Timely Indicator for Economic Outlook based on Swiss Newspaper Articles
affiliations: Swiss National Bank, , ETH Zurich, Swiss National Bank and Swiss National Bank

detail.title: NEOS - A Timely Indicator for Economic Outlook based on Swiss Newspaper Articles

publicationDetails.detailsText: Swiss National Bank Economic Note No. 01/2026
publicationDetails.journalName: Swiss National Bank Economic Note Series

detail.abstract: This note presents the News-based Economic Outlook for Switzerland (NEOS), a timely indicator for the sentiment regarding the economic outlook based on a comprehensive sample of Swiss newspaper articles. The indicator combines machine learning methods and large language models to assess macroeconomic developments in real time. We illustrate the use of NEOS by showing how U.S. tariff announcements shifted the sentiment regarding the economic outlook in Swiss news.

title: Green Banking and Sustainable Development: A Systematic Review of Global Practices and Policy Trends
affiliations: Davangere University and Davangere University

detail.title: Green Banking and Sustainable Development: A Systematic Review of Global Practices and Policy Trends

publicationDetails.detailsText: OIDA International Journal of Sustainable Development, 19 (03), 11-18, 2026
publicationDetails.journalName: OIDA International Journal of Sustainable Development

detail.abstract: This paper systematically reviews global green banking practices and their role in promoting sustainable development. Using conceptual lenses such as the Triple Bottom Line, Stakeholder Theory, and Institutional Theory, the review explores how banks integrate environmental, social, and governance (ESG) criteria into operations. Case examples from developed (EU, USA, UK) and emerging economies (India, China, Brazil) highlight regulatory frameworks, policy trends, and institutional initiatives such as green bonds, climate risk assessment, and ESG disclosures. The study outlines key benefits including brand trust, climate risk mitigation, and access to green capital. It also discusses challenges such as greenwashing, lack of standardization, and limited technical capacity. Future directions recommend global taxonomies, capacity-building initiatives, fintech integration, and regulatory incentives. The review underscores the strategic importance of green banking in advancing the global sustainability agenda.

title: Monetary Policy and Endogenous Crisis Contagion across Borders

authors.last_name: Institute for Monetary and Financial Research

affiliations: (HKIMR)

detail.title: Monetary Policy and Endogenous Crisis Contagion across Borders

publicationDetails.detailsText: Hong Kong Institute for Monetary and Financial Research (HKIMR) Research Paper No. 17/2025
publicationDetails.journalName: Hong Kong Institute for Monetary & Financial Research (HKIMR) Research Paper Series

detail.abstract:
This research paper is written by Frédéric Boissay (Bank for International Settlements), Guangyu Nie (Shanghai University of Finance and Economics), and Changhua Yu (Peking University).

This paper studies a two-country monetary model with an endogenous financial crisis. The financial crisis is induced by a domestic credit crunch, which is tied to the real return on capital in a country. In an open economy environment, we find that exchange rate movements and pass-throughs, the degree of international risk sharing, trade openness, and monetary policy stance in a country significantly affects crisis contagion across borders. A negative supply-side shock in the home country reduces the price of foreign goods, which in turn lowers capital returns in the foreign country, and consequently a crisis may follow. A lower degree of trade openness reduces crisis contagion. A more aggressive ‘leaning against wind’ monetary policy may result in a crisis in both countries due to a demand contraction and exchange rate movements. International risk sharing could hedge moderate shocks but may also generate financial contagion. Limited exchange rate pass-through under LCP may lead to a crisis spillover as well.

title: Nonparametric Identification of Demand without Exogenous Product Characteristics
affiliations: University of California, Berkeley, Stanford University, Brown University and Stanford University

detail.title: Nonparametric Identification of Demand without Exogenous Product Characteristics

publicationDetails.detailsText: NBER Working Paper No. w34842
publicationDetails.journalName: NBER Working Paper Series

detail.abstract:
We study identification of differentiated product demand from market-level data when product characteristics can be endogenous. Past work suggests nonparametric identification may be impossible: that is, in addition to standard price instruments, exogenous characteristic-based instruments are essentially necessary to identify sufficiently flexible demand models with standard index restrictions. We show, however, that price counterfactuals are nonparametrically identified using recentered instruments—which combine exogenous price instruments with possibly endogenous product characteristics—under a weaker index restriction and a new condition we term faithfulness. We argue that faithfulness, like the usual completeness condition for nonparametric instrumental variable identification, is best viewed as a technical requirement on the strength of identifying variation rather than a substantive economic or statistical restriction. We show the two conditions are closely related, though generally distinct. We conclude with several practical implications for the parametric estimation of demand counterfactuals.

Institutional subscribers to the NBER working paper series, and residents of developing countries may download this paper without additional charge at www.nber.org.

title: Corporate Disenfranchisement
affiliations: Hofstra University - Maurice A. Deane School of Law and Southern Methodist University - Dedman School of Law

detail.title: Corporate Disenfranchisement

publicationDetails.detailsText: SMU Dedman School of Law Legal Studies Research Paper No. 722
publicationDetails.journalName: Southern Methodist University Dedman School of Law Legal Studies Research Paper Series

publicationDetails.detailsText: Hofstra Univ. Legal Studies Research Paper
publicationDetails.journalName: Hofstra University - Maurice A. Deane School of Law Legal Studies Research Paper Series

detail.abstract:
Everything must change to keep everything the same. In 2025, the Business Roundtable launched a campaign to eliminate shareholder proposals and Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) Chair Paul Atkins declared “de-politicizing shareholder meetings” a top priority. Also in 2025, the SEC withdrew from its gatekeeping function for shareholder proposals under SEC Rule 14a-8; Texas enacted a million-dollar ownership threshold for shareholder proposals; and President Trump issued an executive order calling on the SEC to repeal or amend Rule 14a-8. These are not aberrations. They are paradigmatic responses to perceived empowerment of the everyday person in corporate governance. It is corporate disenfranchisement by design. Shareholder proposals are the miners’ canary of corporate disenfranchisement: when those in power subject participation to deterring requirements and formalities, ordinary shareholders are silenced. 

This Article fills a critical gap in corporate governance literature. While fierce debates have sought to establish primacy between directors and shareholders, a quiet but critical paradigm has ensured that dominant interests within the corporate establishment retain power over Corporate America. These theoretical accounts assume that formal structures determine who wields influence. They do not. Formal structure differs from actual power. The paradigm we identify demonstrates how dominant interests adapt to governance changes to retain control over the corporate sector. This capture afflicts any participatory system where formal rights threaten control. The result is the systematic exclusion of ordinary shareholders from meaningful governance participation despite their formal rights.

 This Article identifies a pattern recurring across centuries and institutional contexts, tracing the arc of shareholder voice from the robust participatory governance of the East India Company and antebellum American corporations to its post-Civil War decline and the progressive erosion of SEC Rule 14a-8. The paradigm explains how governance models are adapted to entrench power while preserving democratic appearances—the defining mechanism of corporate disenfranchisement.

title: Assessing the Benefits of International Portfolio Diversification: The Case of EMEs in the Era of Geo-economic Fragmentation

authors.last_name: Institute for Monetary and Financial Research

affiliations: (HKIMR)

detail.title: Assessing the Benefits of International Portfolio Diversification: The Case of EMEs in the Era of Geo-economic Fragmentation

publicationDetails.detailsText: Hong Kong Institute for Monetary and Financial Research (HKIMR) Research Paper No. 18/2025
publicationDetails.journalName: Hong Kong Institute for Monetary & Financial Research (HKIMR) Research Paper Series

detail.abstract:
This research paper is written by Wu Shui Tang, Gabriel (Hong Kong Monetary Authority) and Lam Lok Hang, Stephen (Hong Kong Monetary Authority).

This study assesses the benefits of international portfolio diversification for emerging market economies (EMEs) amid rising risks of geo-economic fragmentation. Analysing the risk-adjusted returns as measured by an annualized Sharpe ratio of optimised international stock market portfolios for 20 EMEs from 2014 to 2024, we find that unrestricted investments from EMEs to global equity markets enhance the average risk-adjusted returns by 0.31 compared to a domestic portfolio average of 0.13. This result underscores the importance of opening access to foreign investments for EME investors to maximise diversification benefits. However, we find that rising geo-economic fragmentation could reduce such gains. Restrictions on investments in countries with the largest geopolitical distances from the sampled EMEs, as indicated by low bilateral correlations in UN General Assembly voting outcomes, could reduce the gains by 70%, reducing the Sharpe ratio improvement to 0.09. This reflects a reduced ability to mitigate their exposure to domestic institutional risks, such as those associated with domestic political risks and business environments. Nevertheless, we find that even under such constraints, EME investors could still achieve some diversification benefits by investing in peers with smaller geopolitical distance, particularly those that have more developed financial markets and fewer similarities in terms of their risk profile.

title: Global Portfolio Demand and U.S. Real Interest Rates
affiliations: University of Nevada Las Vegas

detail.title: Global Portfolio Demand and U.S. Real Interest Rates
detail.abstract: This paper studies the role of foreign demand for U.S. Treasury securities in shaping movements in U.S. long-term real interest rates. We develop an empirical framework that decomposes monthly innovations in the 10-year real yield into a component explained by domestic macroeconomic fundamentals and a non-domestic residual component. Using an instrumental-variables strategy to identify exogenous variation in foreign demand, we show that this non-domestic component responds systematically to foreign portfolio demand for U.S. Treasuries. Although domestic factors account for most of the variation in real-yield changes, foreign demand explains a meaningful share of the residual variation that is orthogonal to domestic fundamentals. A variance decomposition quantifies the contribution of this channel and shows that it is stable across alternative specifications, measurement choices, and samples. While the estimated monthly effects are modest, their persistence implies economically significant movements in long-term real rates. These findings have implications for how low long-term real interest rates are interpreted in empirical macro-finance applications. In particular, observed declines in long-term real yields-and natural-rate estimates inferred from them-need not reflect changes in domestic equilibrium forces alone, but may also embed global portfolio-demand pressures for safe U.S. assets. The results highlight the role of global financial integration in shaping U.S. real interest rates and caution against interpreting movements in real yields solely through a domestic lens.

title: Time-Varying Market Sensitivity to Macro News and Monetary Policy: The Role of Attention

authors.last_name: Institute for Monetary and Financial Research

affiliations: (HKIMR)

detail.title: Time-Varying Market Sensitivity to Macro News and Monetary Policy: The Role of Attention

publicationDetails.detailsText: Hong Kong Institute for Monetary and Financial Research (HKIMR) Research Paper No. 21/2025
publicationDetails.journalName: Hong Kong Institute for Monetary & Financial Research (HKIMR) Research Paper Series

detail.abstract:
This research paper is written by Xueliang Wang (University of California, Irvine).

Market sensitivity to macroeconomic announcements (e.g., payrolls, CPI) varies substantially over time. Focusing on interest rate responses, I document that sensitivity increases during periods of high inflation, rising unemployment, and when the Federal Reserve emphasizes macroeconomic conditions. To uncover the fundamental drivers, I distinguish between two hypotheses—changes in investor attention and variations in the perceived data dependence of the monetary policy rule—using an empirical strategy based on their differing implications for the transmission of monetary policy. Consistent with the attention hypothesis, I find that the impact of FOMC announcements is amplified in periods when market sensitivity to macroeconomic announcements is high. A standard New Keynesian model with cognitive discounting is used to illustrate the differences between the two mechanisms. Overall, this paper highlights the role of attention in the effectiveness of monetary policy and macro dynamics.

title: Wealth Tax Primer
affiliations: Stanford University - Hoover Institution, Stanford Graduate School of Business,  and Stanford University - Hoover Institution

detail.title: Wealth Tax Primer
detail.abstract:
This primer examines the administrative, empirical, and economic case against wealth taxation at the state and national levels. Wealth taxes emerged in earlier fiscal systems where tangible, immobile assets were the most feasible tax base. As financial markets expanded and capital became more mobile, advanced economies shifted toward income and consumption taxes, and most countries that experimented with modern wealth taxes ultimately repealed them after encountering administrative complexity, capital flight, and limited revenues.

Drawing on historical and empirical evidence, we document that wealth tax revenue estimates lack credibility because these estimates rely on untested assumptions about asset valuation and taxpayer behavior. High-income and high-net-worth taxpayers are particularly responsive to wealth taxation, so subsequent adoption of wealth taxes by jurisdictions lead to the erosion of the wealth tax and other tax bases, in addition to political pressure to expand the scope of the tax over time. Wealth taxes also distort incentives to save, invest, and build businesses, with implications for long-term capital formation and economic growth for the adopting jurisdictions.

Finally, we review the intellectual foundations of contemporary wealth tax advocacy and conclude that renewed interest in wealth tax proposals reflects political pressure rather than new evidence of effectiveness.

title: Closed-end Mutual Fund Performance and Portfolio Effects
affiliations: University at Albany (SUNY) and State University of New York at Albany - School of Business

detail.title: Closed-end Mutual Fund Performance and Portfolio Effects

declarations.funderStatement: University at Albany Center for Institutional Investment Management

detail.abstract: We find that a majority of US closed-end mutual funds (CEFs) generate positive benchmark-adjusted returns, after expenses. This result is driven mostly by US Muni funds -- the largest subsample -- and shows evidence of persistence at the portfolio level. However, CEFs are frequently levered, so after risk adjustment the outperformance largely vanishes. We further document that CEFs charge investors an average of 4.6% for their management of active share. Finally, we posit that the time-varying pricing discounts of CEFs relative to net asset value (NAV) may contribute to improved portfolio performance in a mean-variance context. Our results show that adding high-discount and low-expense CEFs to a traditional indexed bond/stock portfolio produces higher Sharpe ratios.

title: Climate Policy Uncertainty and Directed Technical Change: Evidence from European Firms

detail.title: Climate Policy Uncertainty and Directed Technical Change: Evidence from European Firms
detail.abstract: In this paper, I derive novel indexes of Climate Policy Uncertainty for four European countries. Exploiting a new dataset of web-scraped newspaper archives and text-as-data techniques, I explore the role of policy stance underlying aggregate indices of CPU, deriving sub-indexes for uncertainty suggesting increasing or decreasing future stringency. Building on the Directed Technical Change literature, I test empirically the relationship between CPU sub-indexes and environmentally sensitive technologies, in a panel of European firms between 1990 and 2020. I find a significant relationship between the direction of firms' technological efforts, proxied by patents, and that of policy uncertainty. The results suggest that policy uncertainty is a relevant factor in affecting the direction of technical change, bearing important implications in terms of both climate and green industrial policy making.

title: Balancing the Books: Immigration and Local Finances in France

detail.title: Balancing the Books: Immigration and Local Finances in France

publicationDetails.detailsText: LEM Discussion Paper Series, N°2026-01, Lille Economie Management (LEM).

detail.abstract: This paper studies the effect of immigration on local public finances in France, combining population census data with municipal budget accounts over the period 2007-2017. To address the endogeneity of immigrants' location choices, I use an instrumental variables strategy based on historical settlement patterns by skill and nationality groups. The results show that immigration has a positive effect on per capita operating net revenues, as well as on both operating revenues and expenditures. Over the period under study, the immigrant share increased on average by 1.38 percentage points, from 8.63% to 10.00%, implying an estimated increase of 2.53% in total operating revenues per capita and 2.45% in total operating expenditures per capita. Immigration is also associated with higher investment activity. Overall, municipalities are able to maintain budgetary balance. Although migration is associated with higher debt levels, improvements in liquidity and self-financing capacity suggest that migration contributes to an expansion of local fiscal capacity.

title: The Sabbath Was Made For Man: On Dynamic Stability as a Metaethical Criterion
affiliations: SUNY College at Brockport and SUNY College at Brockport

detail.title: The Sabbath Was Made For Man: On Dynamic Stability as a Metaethical Criterion
detail.abstract: This paper argues that a rule, to have normative force, must provide for its own persistence, and shows that the axiomatic-universalist approach of modern moral philosophy cannot do so. If this is the case, evolutionary stability logic limits the space of valid moral norms, and demands at least enough parochiality in moral obligations to maintain the assortativity of moral communities. Influential moral frameworks such as Singer's effective altruism and Benatar's antinatalism are ruled out. Partiality is thus understood not as a moral failure, but as constitutive of moral behavior, although there are failure modes when circles of obligation conflict. The paper concludes with a challenge to adherents of modern moral ideologies that the persistence of their moral community as such is a valid, urgent, and sometimes even overriding, moral concern.

title: Trading Goods for Lives: NAFTA’s Mortality Impacts and Implications
affiliations: Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT) - Department of Economics, University of Chicago - Booth School of Business and Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT)

detail.title: Trading Goods for Lives: NAFTA’s Mortality Impacts and Implications

publicationDetails.detailsText: NBER Working Paper No. w34855
publicationDetails.journalName: NBER Working Paper Series

detail.abstract:
We estimate the mortality impact of local labor market exposure to the 1994 North American Free Trade Agreement (NAFTA) as well as to other local area shocks, and provide a parsimonious empirical explanation for differently-signed mortality estimates across different sources of local labor market contractions. Leveraging spatial variation in exposure to Mexican important competition from NAFTA, we find that more exposed areas experienced larger increases in mortality. In the 15 years post-NAFTA, an area with average NAFTA exposure experienced an increase in annual, age-adjusted mortality of 0.68 percent (standard error = 0.19), an increase that more than erases prior estimates of the welfare gains from NAFTA’s nationwide economic benefits. Mortality increases appear across all broad age by sex groups, but are particularly pronounced among working-age men, a demographic that also experienced disproportionate NAFTA-induced declines in (primarily manufacturing) employment. Additional evidence from other local labor market shocks reveals a systematic pattern: declines in local area manufacturing employment increase mortality, while declines in local area non-manufacturing employment decrease mortality. These findings suggest that the sign and magnitude of any mortality impacts of future economic shocks likely depends critically on the extent to which employment declines are concentrated in the manufacturing sector.

Institutional subscribers to the NBER working paper series, and residents of developing countries may download this paper without additional charge at www.nber.org.

title: Building Pro-Worker Artificial Intelligence
affiliations: Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT) - Department of Economics, Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT) - Department of Economics and Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT) - Entrepreneurship Center

detail.title: Building Pro-Worker Artificial Intelligence

publicationDetails.detailsText: NBER Working Paper No. w34854
publicationDetails.journalName: NBER Working Paper Series

detail.abstract:
This paper defines pro-worker technologies, including Artificial Intelligence, as technologies that make human skills and expertise more valuable by expanding worker capabilities. Our conceptual framework distinguishes among five categories of technological change: labor-augmenting, capital-augmenting, automating, expertise-leveling, and new task-creating. Only the last category is unambiguously pro-worker, generating demand for novel human expertise rather than commodifying it. We illustrate these distinctions through hypothetical and real-world examples spanning aviation maintenance, electrical services, custodial work, education, patent examination, and gig delivery. While AI’s capacity to automate work is substantial, we argue that its potential to serve as a collaborator, by extending human judgment, enabling new tasks, and accelerating skill acquisition, is equally transformative and currently underexploited. We identify market failures, including misaligned firm and developer incentives, path dependence, and a pervasive pro-automation ideology, that may lead to underinvestment in pro-worker AI. We consider nine policy directions that would change incentives, including targeted investments in health care and education, tax code reform, antitrust enforcement, and intellectual property protections for worker expertise.

Institutional subscribers to the NBER working paper series, and residents of developing countries may download this paper without additional charge at www.nber.org.

title: Optimal Liquidation in a Defaultable Market
affiliations: Centro de Investigacion en Matematicas (CIMAT), National Research University – Higher School of Economics (HSE University) and Centro de Investigacion en Matematicas (CIMAT) - Department of Probability and Statistics

detail.title: Optimal Liquidation in a Defaultable Market
detail.abstract: In this paper we address the problem of optimal liquidation of a large portfolio composed by securities exposed to default risk. The default time is described in terms of a Brownian motion representing the evolution of the value of the firm, whose assets are available in the market for investors. Considering that selling a large number of assets has a significant impact in the price, and hence in the portfolio's value, the control problem involved to describe the optimal strategy to liquidate a large position is analyzed. Under suitable assumptions in the model, an explicit solution is given to the value function and a precise description of the optimal strategy is obtained.

title: Europe's Productive Capital Gap: Mobilizing Pension and Household Savings to Scale up Risk Capital
affiliations: McGill University, McGill University - Desautels Faculty of Management, McGill University and McGill University

detail.title: Europe's Productive Capital Gap: Mobilizing Pension and Household Savings to Scale up Risk Capital

declarations.declarationOfInterest: We thank the Luxembourg Fund Industry Association (ALFI) for its support.
declarations.funderStatement: The study was funded by the Luxembourg Fund Industry Association (ALFI). The opinions expressed remain solely those of the authors and do not necessarily reflect those of ALFI.

detail.abstract: Europe's productive capital gap reflects a shortage of "risk capital": equity-like capital that drives long-term growth. Lessons from Australia, Canada, and Sweden, which shifted in the 1990s from pay-as-you-go (PAYG) systems to partly funded models, show the potential for reform. Three decades later, these countries hold two to three times more risk capital per worker than PAYG systems in France and Germany. Higher funding levels support greater equity exposure, which compounds over time, and household familiarity with risky assets further boosts voluntary equity saving. Despite different reform paths, successful models share common features: scale, cost efficiency, strong governance, broad coverage, portability, and well-designed incentives. These lessons point to pathways for Europe to mobilize savings and expand its supply of risk capital.

title: Government Funding and the Direction of Academic Energy Research
affiliations: Syracuse University - Department of Public Administration, University of Wisconsin-Madison, Syracuse University and University of Colorado at Boulder

detail.title: Government Funding and the Direction of Academic Energy Research

publicationDetails.detailsText: NBER Working Paper No. w34856
publicationDetails.journalName: NBER Working Paper Series

detail.abstract:
Does government funding influence the choice of research topics? Novel grant-making modalities such as the Advanced Research Projects Agency-Energy (ARPA-E) program aim to encourage scientists to take on difficult-to-solve, wicked societal problems such as clean energy. Yet little causal evidence exists linking funding and research direction, with most existing studies focusing on health sciences. We provide new evidence on the effect of funding on clean energy research, addressing two questions: (1) Do scientists change the focus of their research in response to targeted government funding opportunities? (2) If so, what types of calls for funding best attract new researchers? Using data on grants from the Department of Energy and National Science Foundation, we combine text and regression analyses to compare the publication trajectories of funded scientists to a set of matched controls. After funding, the research of funded scientists becomes more similar to the grant topic than that of the matched controls. The effect is largest for ARPA-E, which explicitly aims to attract new scientists to clean energy research, suggesting that agency efforts to attract new researchers to a topic area can succeed. General calls for funding such as offered by traditional NSF directorates generate less movement.

Institutional subscribers to the NBER working paper series, and residents of developing countries may download this paper without additional charge at www.nber.org.

title: Closed Doors and Quiet Policies: United States V. Louis Rupp, Ii and the Unwritten Rules of Housing Discrimination
affiliations: Southern University Law Center

detail.title: Closed Doors and Quiet Policies: United States V. Louis Rupp, Ii and the Unwritten Rules of Housing Discrimination
detail.abstract:
This Article examines the persistence of familial-status discrimination in the modern rental market and argues that its contemporary form—what this Article terms soft gatekeeping—operates through unwritten rules, discretionary refusals, and plausibly deniable practices rather than explicit exclusion. While the Fair Housing Act (FHA) formally prohibits discrimination against families with children, enforcement has lagged behind the evolution of bias from overt “no children” policies to quiet refusals delivered through timing, tone, and selective justification.

Using United States v. Louis Rupp, II as a doctrinal anchor, this Article demonstrates how courts can recognize and remedy familial-status discrimination even when it is expressed through individualized decisions rather than formal policies. The Eighth Circuit’s decision confirms that FHA liability turns on risk awareness and differential treatment—not on the scale of the landlord or the visibility of the exclusion—and that punitive damages remain an essential deterrent against deliberate yet understated violations.

Building on this foundation, the Article defends soft gatekeeping as a legally cognizable phenomenon and shows how it can be proven through paired testing, temporal and comparative analysis, and pretext scrutiny under familiar burden-shifting frameworks. It further situates familial-status discrimination within layered exclusion, demonstrating how “no children” practices intersect with race-coded steering and source-of-income bias to produce cumulative denials that evade detection when viewed in isolation.

Finally, the Article offers a practical enforcement blueprint—professionalized testing protocols, transactional data capture, fee-shifting settlement architecture, and municipal compliance norms—to translate FHA doctrine into durable access. By naming and proving soft gatekeeping, this Article argues, courts and advocates can restore the FHA’s remedial force and ensure that equal housing opportunity reaches not only large corporate landlords, but the duplex down the block and every family seeking a place to call home.

title: Insurance as National Infrastructure (INANI): A Framework for Economic Growth, Transparency, and Systemic Resilience

detail.title: Insurance as National Infrastructure (INANI): A Framework for Economic Growth, Transparency, and Systemic Resilience
detail.abstract: This paper proposes a reconceptualization of insurance as national infrastructure rather than a discretionary financial product. Drawing on recent advances in digital public infrastructure, the study introduces a Transaction-Based Premium (TBP) model in which a nominal, near-frictionless micro-cess is applied to all formal economic transactions and pooled into a universal national risk fund. Unlike traditional insurance systems that rely on opt-in participation, delayed claims, and fragmented coverage, the TBP framework embeds risk protection directly into the economic bloodstream of the nation. Using India as the primary institutional context-given its Aadhaar-enabled identity layer, real-time payment systems, and direct benefit transfer architecture-the paper argues that universal, automated insurance coverage can reduce household risk aversion, unlock dormant capital, lower fraud through parametric and auditable claims, and accelerate human capital formation. The analysis further explores secondary macroeconomic effects, including improved labor productivity, higher entrepreneurial activity, reduced fiscal shock absorption costs, and enhanced international trust reflected in tourism inflows and passport strength. The paper does not claim that any major economy has fully implemented such a system to date. However, it demonstrates that components of the proposed framework already exist in partial form across India, the United States, Singapore, and select OECD economies. The contribution of this study lies in integrating these components into a single, scalable institutional design and presenting insurance as a proactive nation-building instrument rather than a reactive welfare mechanism.

title: Every Day is January 6: How a Single Event Became America's Insurrection Template

detail.title: Every Day is January 6: How a Single Event Became America's Insurrection Template
detail.abstract:
The events of January 6, 2021, were widely and properly condemned as criminal and unlawful. Acts of violence, intimidation, and interference with a constitutionally prescribed process warranted prosecution under existing law. This paper does not relitigate culpability or contest the seriousness of that conduct. Instead, it examines a structural shift that followed January 6: the transformation of insurrection from a conduct-bound legal category into a date-bound classificatory designation.

Drawing on statutory language, historical usage, and institutional practice, the paper argues that January 6 functioned as a rhetorical demarcation point that altered how political disorder is labeled across time. Through two interacting mechanisms—Retroactive Moral Reclassification and the Selective Freeze—earlier unrest was repositioned within a new moral hierarchy without relabeling, while subsequent unrest exhibiting similar variables was largely insulated from insurrectionary classification. The result is an asymmetric application of an extraordinary category whose thresholds no longer track conduct alone.

The paper formalizes this asymmetry through a symmetry test that holds constant key variables associated with insurrectionary classification—such as duration, coordination, institutional targeting, and displacement of authority—while varying political alignment. When applied, the test suggests that insurrection now functions less as a neutral descriptor than as a politically contingent designation.

The paper concludes by examining the institutional and governance consequences of this shift, including erosion of legal predictability, distortion of enforcement narratives, altered protest incentives, and declining confidence in category neutrality. It argues that while democratic systems can survive protest, unrest, and even episodic political violence, they cannot long sustain extraordinary legal categories that apply only once, to one side, and forever thereafter.

detail.abstract: In the discussion surrounding climate policy, green subsidies are often met with high public support, whereas more efficient carbon pricing is significantly less popular. Using a large-scale survey experiment conducted in Germany, we show that this gap between public preferences and efficient climate policymaking is partially driven by the asymmetric salience of costs and benefits of both instruments. When asked to choose a combination of carbon pricing and green subsidies, the respondents' preferred share of carbon pricing increases when treated with salient information. The more costly (i.e., inefficient) green subsidies are compared to carbon pricing, the stronger the effect. However, our study also shows that preferences for green subsidies are sticky, resulting in a substantial willingness to pay for subsidies and overall higher costs of climate policy. This subsidy preference is persistent even if respondents do not rely on fossil fuels for heating.

title: Interest Rates and Equity Valuations
affiliations: University of Chicago - Booth School of Business and University of California, Berkeley - Haas School of Business - Finance Group

detail.title: Interest Rates and Equity Valuations
detail.abstract: A large body of work has sought to measure the effect of interest rates on equity valuations. The challenge in doing so is that both are endogenous, and their comovement depends on the forces driving interest-rate changes. To address this problem, we develop and estimate a decomposition that splits movements in real rates into three structural drivers: changes in expected growth, risk, or "pure discounting." We show that only pure discount-rate shocks transmit one-for-one to equity valuations, with little or negative transmission of growth and risk shocks. Implementing our decomposition with a global panel of growth expectations and asset prices, we find a weak unconditional relation between valuations and real rates but a strong relation with the pure discounting component, which explains 80% of cross-country valuation changes since 1990. In the U.S., we find that 35% of the interest-rate decline is attributable to pure discounting, implying that only a fraction of the change in rates has passed through directly to equities. We use the decomposition to revisit evidence on the role of interest rates in explaining price variation, and to study higher-frequency returns, cross-sectional rate exposures, duration-matched equity premia, and reactions to monetary policy.

detail.abstract: This paper provides a detailed financial, risk, and regulatory analysis of the collapse of Silicon Valley Bank in March 2023 in the form of a case study seminar paper. By analyzing original horizontal and vertical financial analysis with figured sought from 10-K filings between 2018 and 2022, and other regulatory reports and published papers, the case uncovers a strategic pivot toward long-duration, HTM securities that created a duration gap that the bank could not stand. An important finding made in this paper shows that according to the Adjusted CET1 Ratio, using the CET1 figures of the bank, not the group, SVB was technically insolvent on a markto-market basis before its public failure. The paper concludes that a combination of concentrated uninsured deposits, digital-age bank run velocity, and lagging regulatory oversight converged to trigger the largest bank failure in U.S. modern history.

detail.abstract: This paper critically examines the prevailing narrative that the crisis of U.S. dollar hegemony is primarily a failure of international trust. By analyzing the structural resilience of the dollar-centric system following the 1971 Nixon Shock, this study argues that the dollar's dominance remains anchored in three structural variables: the absorptive capacity of the U.S. domestic market, the absence of viable institutional and monetary alternatives, and the path dependence of global trade. The analysis demonstrates that current global instabilities stem not from functional flaws within the currency itself, but from the erosion of domestic political consensus within the United States regarding the costs of acting as the "Order Manager." Specifically, the study highlights the tension between domestic prosperity and the sustained trade deficits required to provide global liquidity-a modern manifestation of the Triffin Dilemma. The paper concludes that the future of the international monetary order is a strategic policy choice rather than an inevitability, contingent upon the willingness of U.S. leadership to bear the economic and political burdens of maintaining the global order through a managed realignment.

title: Human Rights Universalism and Domestic Democratic Cohesion in U.S. Grand Strategy: A Dynamic Two-Level Analysis

detail.title: Human Rights Universalism and Domestic Democratic Cohesion in U.S. Grand Strategy: A Dynamic Two-Level Analysis
detail.abstract: This article examines the evolution of the strategic role of human rights in U.S. grand strategy following the weakening of their universalist function within the post-1945 international order. It conceptualizes universalism not as a purely moral doctrine, but as a historically contingent configuration through which power was translated into legitimacy and order-making. Drawing on a qualitative analysis of National Security Strategies and key presidential articulations, the article traces how the positioning of human rights evolved across successive historical junctures. It then analyses the parallel transformation of domestic democratic cohesion in the United States, focusing on long-term processes of polarization, legitimacy strain, and institutional fragmentation. By integrating these two dimensions, the article advances a time-sensitive interpretation of their interaction, showing how shifting domestic conditions and external pressures jointly redefined the scope and limits of human rights as mediating principles of international order.

detail.abstract:
Nonprofit organizations, are widely studied in terms of formal governance structures,
compliance, and fiduciary duties, yet many of the practical, everyday mechanisms that
sustain organizational continuity remain overlooked. However, small charities and grant-
dependent associations, often face governance challenges that are invisible yet highly
consequential. While mainstream literature emphasizes board composition, fiduciary
duties, and regulatory compliance, it largely ignores the procedural and infrastructural
dimensions where governance actually operates. This book addresses that gap by
examining the hidden mechanisms through which governance failures occur:
communication practices, recordkeeping systems, and the exercise of authority within
and across boards and staff. Drawing on organizational theory, archival science, and
nonprofit practice, the book highlights how informal processes—such as the use of
personal email accounts for official business, incomplete handovers, unclear signatory
authority, and ambiguous roles of advisory boards—can create risks for accountability,
continuity, and legal compliance. Through detailed analysis and practical guidance, this
volume illuminates the invisible failures that threaten organizational legitimacy, disrupt
succession, and impede mission continuity. By uncovering these overlooked but critical
issues, the book provides nonprofit leaders, boards, and practitioners with a framework
for strengthening governance infrastructure, preserving institutional memory, and
mitigating risk before failures become visible crises.

title: Asset Pricing with Dynamic and Static Investors
affiliations: University of Warwick, Warwick Business School

detail.title: Asset Pricing with Dynamic and Static Investors
detail.abstract: I analytically characterize a tractable model with dynamic investors, whose asset allocation responds to news, and static investors, whose asset allocation remains stable over time. Static investors buy equities to meet pre-specified policy targets, regardless of news about earnings, creating price pressure. Dynamic investors, though unconstrained, do not regard such price pressure as an arbitrage opportunity. They rationally expect it to persist, because static investors adhere consistently to their strategy. In equilibrium, the aggregate valuation of equity assets depends on the level of wealth managed by static investors, over and above dividends, discount rates, and the wealth flows they receive.

detail.abstract: This paper explores the socio-political landscape of Hong Kong in the aftermath of the 2019-2020 protests, focusing on the implications of governance changes and the erosion of civil liberties. The aim is to identify key challenges faced by the region and propose innovative, solution-oriented strategies that promote participatory governance, social justice, and economic resilience. Through a mixed-methods approach, including qualitative interviews and quantitative data analysis, the research examines the motivations behind the protests, the role of technology in mobilization, and the potential for international collaboration. Findings indicate a significant disconnect between government actions and public demands, highlighting the need for inclusive dialogue and policy reform. The overall conclusion emphasizes the importance of fostering civic engagement and resilience in Hong Kong to navigate its complex political landscape and ensure a sustainable future dovetailing with the basic law of the special administrative city and exploiting fully the potential of the situation.

title: Merchant Steering of Consumer Payment Choice

detail.title: Merchant Steering of Consumer Payment Choice

publicationDetails.detailsText: FRB Atlanta Working Paper No. 2026-2
publicationDetails.journalName: Federal Reserve Bank of Atlanta Research Paper Series

detail.abstract: This paper investigates the degree to which merchants influence consumers' choice of how they pay for transactions. Using data from the Survey and Diary of Consumer Payments Choice, we examine consumers' adherence to their preferred payment method when making in-person transactions. We also investigate whether merchants are able to steer consumers away from their preferred payment method. We characterize preferences for paying with cash or cards according to consumers' income, level of education, and employment status. We find that consumers make most payments with their preferred method. When consumers pay with a nonpreferred method, it is due only in small part to merchants' refusal to accept that payment method. If a merchant accepts card payments, consumers who prefer paying with cards are not likely to pay with cash for large-value transactions or for gas or groceries. Discounts on cash purchases do not affect the probability of consumers deviating from using cards and paying with cash. Finally, the paper identifies “inertia” effects, which lead consumers to use the same payment method for consecutive purchases.

title: Does Experience Matter? Past Fraud Experiences, Data Compromises, and Credit Market Behavior
affiliations: Federal Reserve Bank of Philadelphia and Federal Reserve Bank of Kansas City

detail.title: Does Experience Matter? Past Fraud Experiences, Data Compromises, and Credit Market Behavior

publicationDetails.detailsText: FRB of Philadelphia Working Paper No. 26-10
publicationDetails.journalName: Federal Reserve Bank of Philadelphia Working Paper Series

detail.abstract: We study how past experiences with fraud affect individuals’ likelihood of taking precautionary action in credit markets when faced with a new shock that raises their fraud risks. We focus on two kinds of past experiences with fraud: direct experience with fraud and a “near-miss” experience that increased fraud risk but did not directly lead to fraud. Using the 2017 Equifax data breach announcement, we show that individuals with either type of prior experience with fraud were more likely to take a precautionary action — freezing their credit report — than individuals with no prior experience with fraud. We also find that individuals with past direct experience with fraud were more likely to freeze their credit report than individuals who had a past near-miss experience. The individuals who froze their credit report had fewer total accounts and credit inquiries than those who did not, but this reduction in credit did not reduce their credit scores.
